item.title: Dengue surge raises questions over government preparedness
item.description:
Despite repeated outbreaks in previous years and access to historical data, Bangladesh has seen a sharp rise in dengue cases and deaths in 2026. While the seasonal surge during the monsoon is well known, questions have been raised over why effective preventive measures were not taken before infections began to climb.
Concerns have also emerged over whether timely mosquito-control operations and stronger preventive measures could have reduced the number of infections, as well as whether the health and local government ministries have coordinated effectively to prepare for and contain the outbreak. Although dengue cases and deaths in 2026 have increased significantly compared with 2025, the health and local government ministries have cited figures from 2023 to claim that the situation remains better than in previous years.
From January 1 to October 25, Bangladesh recorded 132,948 dengue infections and 384 deaths this year, according to figures cited in the report.
During the same period in 2025, the country recorded 64,297 cases and 259 deaths. In 2024, the figures stood at 54,702 cases and 269 deaths.
Compared with the corresponding period in 2025, dengue cases have increased by 106.8% this year, while deaths have risen by 48.3%. Compared with the same period in 2024, cases have increased by 143% and deaths by 42.8%.
However, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) reported that 123,998 dengue patients were hospitalised between January 1 and October 25, with 384 deaths recorded during the period. The discrepancy between the total case figures cited above and the DGHS hospitalisation data requires verification.
Dhaka Division recorded the highest number of hospitalisations, with 50,292 patients and 183 deaths. Khulna Division ranked second, with 19,092 hospitalisations and 68 deaths.
Chittagong Division reported 18,261 hospitalisations and 37 deaths, while Barisal Division recorded 15,633 hospitalisations and 28 deaths.
Khulna, which ranks second after Dhaka in dengue cases and deaths, has continued mosquito-control and cleanliness drives to curb the outbreak.
Asked about the measures being taken, Khulna Civil Surgeon Dr Md Moniruzzaman said he had joined the post on October 15 and was implementing activities in line with directives from the Ministry of Local Government.
“We are conducting cleanliness drives in areas where stagnant water in ditches, drains and other places could create breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes. These drives continue every day, with intensified efforts on Saturdays,” he said.
He added that reports on the activities were being submitted to the ministry.
“We are coordinating with public and private schools, colleges and other institutions to continue mosquito-control operations,” he said, adding that his predecessor had also carried out similar initiatives.
Experts warn that once dengue begins spreading in an area, bringing the outbreak under control becomes difficult. However, regular mosquito-control operations, proper sanitation, the elimination of breeding grounds and timely public health interventions can help reduce transmission.
The rising number of cases has renewed questions about whether preventive measures were implemented early enough and whether coordination among the relevant authorities has been sufficient to contain the outbreak.
Entomologist Professor Kabirul Bashar said climate change is altering temperature, rainfall and humidity patterns in Bangladesh, affecting the spread of Aedes mosquitoes and the transmission of dengue.
He stressed the need to revise mosquito-control strategies to adapt to changing climatic conditions.
While climate change can be addressed through mitigation and adaptation, large-scale mitigation efforts may be beyond the capacity of agencies responsible for mosquito control. However, authorities can develop adaptation-based strategies by identifying how changes in weather and environmental conditions affect Aedes mosquito behaviour, he said.
Asked about preventive measures taken since the government assumed office, amid a rise in dengue cases and deaths compared with the same period last year despite the availability of historical data, State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam said preventive activities had been ongoing since the beginning of the government's tenure.
“Our responsibility is to take preventive measures, and we have been doing so since taking office. We have undertaken cleanliness drives, awareness campaigns and leaflet distribution,” he said.
He added that the government had decided to launch large-scale awareness campaigns through loudspeaker announcements across city corporations, municipalities, districts and upazilas.
The campaigns aim to raise public awareness and eliminate potential Aedes mosquito breeding grounds, he said.
The state minister also said anti-dengue activities were being conducted every Saturday with the participation of Scouts, Rover Scouts and voluntary organisations. The programme will continue every Saturday until December 12, he added.
Meanwhile, the government has decided to form 20 special monitoring committees across 20 zones of Dhaka North and Dhaka South city corporations to strengthen dengue prevention, improve cleanliness and eliminate mosquito breeding grounds.
Director-level officials from the Prime Minister's Office will lead the committees, which will include representatives from the relevant ministries, Dhaka WASA, the metropolitan police and the city corporations, as well as executive magistrates.
The committees will monitor dengue prevention efforts and oversee intensified cleanliness drives.
Public health expert Dr Mustak Hossain said dengue had become a persistent public health crisis in Bangladesh and could not be controlled through superficial fogging operations or fines alone.
He said the government should have formed a high-level interministerial task force, similar to the one established during the Covid-19 pandemic, and implemented the 2019 national dengue management guidelines at the grassroots level.
He recommended identifying a one-kilometre radius around each confirmed patient's location as a potential hotspot and launching targeted operations to destroy mosquito larvae in line with scientific guidelines.
He also stressed the need to encourage community participation at the ward level, following Kolkata's model, and provide free dengue tests and mosquito nets to low-income patients through public hospitals.
Unless the government adopts a scientific, source-based approach to eliminating mosquito larvae, the country will continue to pay a heavy price for the outbreak, he warned.
State Minister for Health Dr MA Mohit said dengue-prone areas were being identified for mosquito-larvae destruction and cleanliness drives.
Hospitals' patient records are being analysed to identify areas with high infection rates, where special cleanliness drives and larvicide applications are being carried out promptly, he said, adding that city corporations were also involved in the efforts.
“There is no shortage of government initiatives to tackle dengue,” he said.
According to the state minister, weekly meetings are being held with mayors, administrators and officials from the health and local government ministries to review the situation. The prime minister, ministers and state ministers are also discussing the issue regularly.
He claimed that collective efforts had kept the dengue infection rate lower this year than in previous years.
Five more people died of dengue and 1,546 new patients were hospitalized across the country in the 24 hours ending at 8:00am on Monday.
With the latest fatalities, the dengue death toll in the country has risen to 389 this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Among the new deaths, one each was reported in Dhaka, Chittagong, Khulna, Rajshahi and Barisal divisions.
Since January 1 this year, a total of 126,166 dengue patients have been admitted to hospitals across the country. Of them, 119,393 have recovered.

item.title: CPB office attacked in Paltan
item.description:
A group of people attacked Mukti Bhaban, the office of the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB), in Dhaka's Paltan area on Monday night.
The attack took place around 10pm.
The CPB blamed BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami activists for the incident, while BNP activists denied the allegation.
CPB Central Committee President Sazzad Zahir Chandan told Dhaka Tribune that a group of youths had launched a sudden attack on their office.
He blamed BNP and Jamaat activists for the attack, saying the situation stemmed from the detention and subsequent release of former Bangladesh Chhatra Union president Dipak Shil earlier in the evening.
According to Chandan, the attackers accused CPB activists of chanting “Joy Bangla”. He, however, said no such slogan had been chanted from the party office.
Officer-in-Charge of Paltan police station Ariful Islam told Dhaka Tribune that Dipak's supporters had chanted “Joy Bangla” in celebration after he was released from detention.
Angered by the slogans, some people attacked the CPB office, he said.
Police are investigating the incident and have positioned themselves between the two groups to prevent further unrest, he said.

item.title: Tarique, Takaichi to hold bilateral summit in Tokyo Tuesday
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is set to hold a bilateral summit with his Japanese counterpart, Sanae Takaichi, in Tokyo on Tuesday to strengthen the strategic partnership, boost trade and investment, and expand cooperation in key sectors between Bangladesh and Japan.
The meeting will begin at 11:45am local time at the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office, known as the Kantei, following a guard of honour to be given to Tarique Rahman from 11:30am to 11:40am.
The two leaders will hold talks until 12:10pm, followed by a joint press announcement from 12:15pm to 12:25pm.
Takaichi will then host a luncheon for the Bangladesh Prime Minister from 12:30pm to 1:10pm.
At the beginning of the lunch, she is scheduled to deliver a brief welcome remark and propose a toast, followed by a short reply and return toast from Tarique Rahman.
According to Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin, the two leaders will discuss strengthening bilateral relations, expanding business, trade and investment, Japanese cooperation in various sectors and international issues.
At a curtain-raiser press conference back in Dhaka, Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam said the Prime Minister’s four-day visit is expected to open new avenues for bilateral cooperation and attract fresh Japanese private investment in Bangladesh.
He said the talks would focus on the effective implementation of the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market and strengthening business engagement.
The two sides are also expected to explore cooperation in renewable energy, agriculture, science and technology, digital transformation, skills development and human resource development.
Siam said several memorandums of understanding (MoUs) are being discussed for signing during the visit. Draft agreements cover agriculture, fisheries, human resource and skills development, domestic aviation, trade, environmental conservation and the modernisation of local government.
“We hope that many of these MoUs will be signed during the visit,” he said.
During the visit, Tarique Rahman is also scheduled to deliver the keynote address at the Japan-Bangladesh Economic Forum and meet Japanese business leaders.
The prime minister reached Tokyo on Monday morning on a four-day visit at the invitation of Takaichi.
He was received at Narita International Airport by Japanese State Minister for Foreign Affairs Nakasone Yasutaka.
Tarique Rahman is leading a high-level delegation that includes Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, and Prime Minister’s Adviser on Posts, Telecommunications, ICT and Science and Technology Rehan Asif Asad.
Invest Bangladesh Authority Chairman Ashik Chowdhury, Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman, Prime Minister’s Special Assistant for Overseas Employment in the Asia-Pacific Region Dr Md Shakirul Islam Khan, Foreign Secretary Siam, Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury, Economic Relations Division Secretary Shahriar Kader Siddiky and Prime Minister’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon are among other delegation members.
Hefazat-e-Islam Joint Secretary General and Nezame Islam Party acting Secretary General Azizul Hoque Islamabadi, and Am Janata Dal General Secretary Md Tarek Rahman are also accompanying the Prime Minister.
This is Tarique’s third state visit abroad since taking office on February 17 this year. He previously made state visits to Malaysia and China, and travelled to New York, the United States, in September to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

item.title: Karnaphuli Garden City shopping complex closes after business downturn
item.description:
Once a popular shopping destination in the capital, Karnaphuli Garden City has remained closed since October 1 amid a business downturn, declining customer numbers and mounting unpaid bills.
During a visit on Monday, the shopping complex's main entrance was found shut, with a banner announcing: “The shopping complex will remain closed from October 1, 2026.”
According to those concerned, the 20-storey building was established by Karnaphuli Group at the Shantinagar-Kakrail intersection in 1998. The shopping mall occupied the ground floor through the 3rd floor, while the 4th floor housed a food court and garden.
The complex initially had 198 shops. However, by the time it closed, only 17 shops inside the complex and 25 in total, including those outside, remained open.
Bakibillah Osmani, general secretary of the owners’ association, told Dhaka Tribune that the closure resulted from a decade of mismanagement, the country's economic downturn and a lack of business.
He said: “This did not happen in a single day. Whether you call it a decade of mismanagement, the country's economic downturn or a lack of business, all these factors have contributed to this situation over the past decade.”
He said the difficult period began around 2016–17, when the Shantinagar flyover was constructed. Some shop owners who also owned the businesses operating there moved to other markets, expecting to return if the complex reopened or road conditions improved.
According to him, road closures during flyover construction reduced customer numbers. Established businesses moved to other markets and did not return. The Covid-19 pandemic further worsened the situation.
He said: “When the market reopened, the traders did not return. They had settled in other markets. Then the pandemic, Covid, came. During that period, some traders closed their shops permanently. Gradually, the shops began to close. On the day we closed the market, only 17 shops inside were open. Including those outside, the total was 25.”
Describing the complex's financial situation, Bakibillah Osmani said monthly expenses, including electricity bills and staff salaries, exceeded Tk15 lakh.
He said: “We were receiving a maximum of Tk1 lakh to Tk1.5 lakh in service charges.”
The complex's outstanding electricity bills have reportedly exceeded Tk50 lakh.
He had previously said: “Service charges were not coming in, and the outstanding electricity bill had reached around Tk50 lakh. As a result, all the owners jointly decided to close the market.”
He also said the complex had been operating for more than 6 months using money borrowed from market committee officials and some of the owners.

item.title: Minister: Committee to probe freedom fighter’s burial in Pirojpur
item.description:
Liberation War Affairs Minister Ahmed Azam Khan has said a committee will be formed to investigate the incident in Pirojpur in which the wife and daughter of a freedom fighter allegedly dug up his grave and buried him.
He said those responsible would face appropriate action based on the findings of the investigation.
The minister made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists after visiting the Martyred Intellectuals Memorial in Rayerbazar, Dhaka, on Monday.
“I will look into the matter as soon as I return to my office today. I will also speak with the Muktijoddha Sangsad in Pirojpur. We will form a committee to investigate the incident and take appropriate action against those responsible based on the investigation report,” he said.
The minister said Bangladesh is an independent, democratic republic and there is no scope for anyone to take a position against the Liberation War.
He said the Liberation War Affairs Ministry had not been properly informed about the incident involving the freedom fighter.
“If the ministry had been informed, it could have taken the matter into consideration earlier and taken necessary steps,” he said.
Ahmed Azam Khan said some people opposed the Liberation War in 1971 and that he believed those forces remained active in the country.
“They are trying to advance their position through various tactics and, when given the opportunity, attempt to undermine the Liberation War by portraying different movements as a ‘second independence’,” he said.
The minister said the ministry has been working to thwart any conspiracy against the Liberation War and freedom fighters. “We are always prepared to deal with such situations,” he added.

item.title: Climate change leaves coastal elderly isolated
item.description:
In a small, dilapidated shelter beside a canal in Haoladar Bari of Pratapnagar union in Satkhira’s Ashashuni upazila, Shahjahan Ali, in his seventies, and his wife Rabeya Begum, in her sixties, spend their days gazing at the water that has destroyed their lives.
They once owned two bighas of land, a mango orchard, paddy fields and a well-maintained home. But Super Cyclone Amphan in May 2020 breached nearby embankments, allowing saline water from the Kholpetua and Kapatakkha rivers to inundate their homestead and farmland. Repeated flooding gradually destroyed their land and livelihoods.
As river erosion and salinity worsened, their adult sons left in search of work, taking their children with them.
“I miss my grandchildren, but what can we do? They have left in search of work. Where can we go at this age? We once had everything, including our loved ones. Now, there is nobody,” Rabeya said.
Her husband, Shahjahan Ali, recalled how his wife’s family once owned hundreds of bighas of land.
“I can no longer work because of my illness. Whatever our son gives us is not enough to run the household, and we often go hungry. I am tired of this lonely life. Now, I am simply waiting for death,” he said.
Their story reflects a growing crisis along Bangladesh’s southwestern coast, where climate-related disasters are destroying livelihoods, driving migration and leaving elderly people increasingly isolated.
Shamsun Nahar Ratna, a senior scientific officer at the Soil Resource Development Institute’s Satkhira regional office, said salinity in the Kholpetua River had risen from 22-25 decisiemens per metre in 2019 to as high as 50-55 in 2026.
According to Bangladesh’s 2024 Soil Salinity Map, around 1.16 million hectares of the country’s 1.70 million hectares of coastal agricultural land have become severely saline.
Ratna attributed the worsening situation partly to declining upstream river flows, irregular rainfall and the movement of saline water towards the soil surface. The resulting damage to farmland is pushing farmers towards fish and shrimp farming.
According to figures cited in the report, around 2.5 million people were displaced from coastal areas during Amphan in 2020. Data from the International Organization for Migration and the government indicate that approximately 4.96 million people are internally displaced by disasters such as floods, river erosion and storm surges. The World Bank has warned that Bangladesh could have nearly 20 million internal climate migrants by 2050 without effective action.
A joint survey by Satkhira municipality and development organisation Uttaran found that 10,133 families had moved to the district town over 22 years because of natural disasters. Around 84% had lost their homes to river erosion, storm surges and salinity.
Many now live in overcrowded settlements with inadequate housing, sanitation and drainage facilities.
In neighbouring Gabura union of Shyamnagar upazila, 60-year-old Fazila Khatun, a widow who is partially paralysed, struggles to survive after her children left in search of work.
“We used to live by farming. Now there is salt everywhere. Even a vegetable plant cannot survive. We have to walk miles to collect drinking water,” she said.
Environmental activist and researcher Piyush Baulia Pintu blamed repeated cyclones, unplanned shrimp farming and poorly planned sluice gates for weakening embankments. In parts of Gabura, including Durgabati, Harinnagar, Singhortali and Jelekhali, erosion has swallowed homes and entire settlements.
He said some displaced residents had taken out loans to buy vans or venture into unfamiliar occupations but were later forced to leave when they could not repay their debts.
Farida Parvin, a reserved-seat woman member of Gabura union parishad, said climate change, particularly persistent river erosion, tidal surges and severe cyclones, was the main driver of displacement in the area.
“Income-generating opportunities are also extremely limited. Previously, paddy cultivation provided jobs for around 20 labourers during the farming season. But saltwater fish and shrimp farming requires only one worker, leaving the other 19 unemployed and forcing them to leave the area,” she said.
Madhab Chandra Dutta, executive director of human rights organisation Swadesh, said climate change was also causing non-economic losses, including the erosion of cultural identity, mental well-being and social bonds.
Traditional practices such as boat races, folk songs and rituals associated with Bonbibi and Manasa are disappearing as people abandon their ancestral homes and traditional occupations.
Bhakta Munda, a resident of Datinakhali, said the struggle to survive had overshadowed cultural life.
“After Amphan and Yaas, people became so preoccupied with survival that the joy of festivals disappeared. Social bonds among neighbours are also fading,” he said.
Farida Parvin, a reserved-seat woman member of Gabura union parishad, said shrinking employment opportunities were accelerating migration.
“During the paddy cultivation season, around 20 labourers could find work in a field. But shrimp farming can often be managed by just one worker. The others are left without jobs and forced to leave,” she said.
According to Farida, around two in every 10 families in Gabura have relocated, while elderly parents are often left behind without independent sources of income.
Ashik-e-Elahi, convener of the Satkhira Climate Council, said climate change had become a human rights issue. He called for accessible loans and entrepreneurship support to help young people remain in agriculture, alongside greater investment in vulnerable communities.
Dutta urged authorities to build durable concrete-block embankments, rehabilitate displaced families on available government-owned land and create alternative employment opportunities.
Sonia Akter Pushpa, a psychosocial counsellor at Moner Bondhu, said migration was placing severe psychological pressure on women and elderly people left behind. She called for local employment opportunities, regular communication between family members and community-based mental health services.
Without sustained investment in embankments, rehabilitation, livelihoods and psychosocial support, experts warn, coastal communities risk losing not only their homes but also their cultural heritage and social bonds.

item.title: Police release former Chhatra Union president Dipak Shil
item.description:
Police have released Dipak Shil, former president of Bangladesh Chhatra Union, after detaining him during a human chain by artists and cultural activists at Dhanmondi 27 in the capital on Monday.
Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Mohammadpur Police Station Abdul Halim confirmed the matter on Monday night, saying Dipak was freed after questioning.
Chhatra Union Secretary Bahauddin Shuvo also confirmed it in a Facebook post around 9:00pm.
The human chain was organised under the banner of “Protesting Artists and People” to protest attacks on Baul music and other cultural events in different parts of the country in the name of “Tawhidi Janata”.
The programme was scheduled for Monday afternoon on Dhanmondi 27 Road, but police obstructed the gathering and detained Dipak.
Actress Sumana Soma, who attended the programme, said they had gathered to protest attacks on Bauls and obstruction of cultural events across the country.
“When police obstructed us, we protested. Police personnel then dragged us towards their vehicle, while Dipak was taken away in a police van,” she said.
Cultural activist Faruk H Khan condemned the cancellation of Baul music programmes, obstruction of protests by artists and citizens, and alleged interference with the namaz- e- janaza and burial of freedom fighter Manik Pashari.
He said Baul traditions and Bengali culture were facing continued attacks across the country. He also alleged that anti-liberation forces and militant fundamentalist groups were behind the incidents.

item.title: Curriculum reform and the old wounds of a new attempt
item.description:
Today's workforce demands a broad set of competencies: C ritical thinking, problem-solving, communication, empathy, collaboration, adaptability, entrepreneurship, strong reading and writing, digital literacy, and lifelong learning.
Not all of these need to be fully developed at school. Schools lay the foundations; universities and workplaces deepen them. Reading, writing, basic digital skills, communication, empathy and teamwork begin at school. Critical thinking and problem-solving are introduced there but mature later through more independent and open-ended work. Entrepreneurship and self-directed learning also develop through higher education and work experience.
That is the ideal division of labour . The question is whether Bangladeshi schools are laying those foundations.
The gap between design and classroom
Bangladesh has repeatedly tried to build a more competency-based curriculum. Each attempt has promised less rote memorization and more critical thinking and practical learning. But writing a curriculum is easier than delivering it across tens of thousands of schools.
The 2021 competency-based curriculum began to be introduced in 2023, with plans to extend it to Class XII by 2027. Yet even a well-designed curriculum cannot succeed on paper alone. Its success depends on teachers, resources and classroom conditions.
Studies of its implementation identified gaps between what the curriculum expected and what many classrooms could deliver. Teachers were not always adequately prepared. Schools differed greatly in facilities and resources, particularly between urban and rural areas. Teaching materials were sometimes lacking, while textbook delivery was repeatedly delayed.
Consider collaboration. Group work is difficult when one teacher must manage a large class with limited space and materials. Critical thinking is equally difficult to teach if teachers have not been trained to develop it.
Assessment may be the biggest obstacle. Students and families naturally organize their efforts around what is tested. If major examinations continue to reward memorization and reproduction of prepared answers, a competency-based curriculum will struggle to change how students learn.
After reviewing implementation difficulties, the interim government reverted to the previous curriculum in early 2025.
The lesson is clear: C hanging what students are expected to learn is not enough. Reform must also address how learning takes place in the classroom.
The 2026 initiative
The current government has launched another curriculum reform, with a broader overhaul planned for 2028. The government says it is moving more gradually than the previous reform. It has also announced new elements including sports, culture, technical and vocational education, and “Learning with Happiness . ” More recent government statements have also highlighted AI, robotics, machine learning and cybersecurity.
These are useful directions. But they raise a more fundamental question: What should every child be able to do after ten or twelve years of schooling?
A modern curriculum should answer that question clearly. Students need more than subject knowledge. They should be able to think critically, solve unfamiliar problems, communicate clearly, work with others, adapt to change, learn independently and use technology responsibly. They need creativity and initiative, but also empathy, integrity and civic responsibility. They should acquire practical and technical skills while developing the ability to keep learning throughout life.
The government's stated goals already include several of these areas, such as creativity, employability, practical skills and future-oriented technology. The challenge is to turn these aspirations into clearly defined competencies and make sure they are taught across the curriculum rather than left to a few new subjects.
What matters in the classroom
The real test of the new reform will not be the number of new textbooks. It will be whether teachers are prepared before the new curriculum reaches their classrooms; whether schools have the space, equipment and learning materials needed for practical and collaborative work; and whether assessment rewards understanding, reasoning and application rather than memorization .
The government has said the reform will be supported by teacher guides, workbooks, remedial materials and video lessons. These resources can support both teachers and students, but their value will depend on timely delivery and effective use. In particular, teachers need practical guidance on how to use these materials to support classroom learning rather than simply adding more content to what they already teach.
Where teaching methods come in
How teachers teach matters as much as what they teach. A lesson does not have to rely entirely on explanation and note-taking. Teachers can ask questions, encourage short discussions, use simple classroom activities, give students problems to solve, and let them work together and explain their ideas. Such approaches can help students understand and apply what they learn rather than simply remember it. The aim is not to burden teachers with complicated new methods, but to gradually make classrooms more interactive and give students a more active role in learning.
Teachers can also use approaches such as the flipped classroom, project-based learning, and problem-based learning where they are appropriate. However, no single teaching method is suitable for every subject, every topic, or every learner. The choice should depend on what students are expected to learn and which approach is most likely to help them achieve that learning goal. A strong curriculum should therefore give teachers a repertoire of methods and, equally importantly, the training and resources to know when and how to use them.
The real test of reform
The goal should not be another curriculum that looks modern on paper but proves difficult to implement in practice. Nor should reform be reduced to adding new subjects, textbooks or digital materials. Its real measure is whether students leave school able to read and write well, think clearly, solve problems, communicate and collaborate, use technology wisely, adapt to change and act responsibly.
Bangladesh does not need to keep changing the destination. It needs to prepare its teachers, equip its schools and improve what happens in the classroom so that students can actually reach it. The challenge now is not to design another ambitious curriculum, but to build a reliable road from policy to the classroom.
MM Shahidul Hassan is d istinguished p rofessor, Eastern University, and f ormer v ice c hancellor, East West University, Bangladesh .

item.title: Four cigarette price tiers, 12 price points: A system designed for switching, not quitting
item.description:
When cigarette prices rise, smokers are expected to cut consumption or quit. That is the central public-health justification for increasing tobacco taxes. In Bangladesh, however, many smokers can respond in a much simpler way: They can switch to a cheaper brand.
A rapid survey conducted by PROGGA (Knowledge for Progress) in September 2026 shows how easily this can happen. The survey covered 80 cigarette retailers across all eight divisional cities and identified 53 brands being sold at 12 distinct price points.
Yet, officially, Bangladesh has only four cigarette price tiers: Low, medium, high, and premium.
This means that what appears to be a four-tier structure in government policy has become a 12-price-point market in practice. Such a wide range of prices gives smokers ample room to move down the price ladder when their preferred cigarettes become more expensive.
A major loophole in the low tier
The greatest price variation was found in the low tier, where cigarettes were available at eight different price points.
Under the current structure, the minimum retail prices for a pack of 10 cigarettes are Tk65 and above for the low tier, Tk92 and above for the medium tier, Tk160 and above for the high tier, and Tk210 and above for the premium tier.
The problem lies partly in the phrase “and above.”
If the low tier begins at Tk65 and the medium tier begins at Tk92, manufacturers can place low-tier cigarettes at several prices between Tk65 and Tk91. Indeed, the survey found a low-tier cigarette priced at Tk90, only Tk2 below the starting price of the medium tier.
Therefore, a smoker facing a price increase does not necessarily have to quit, reduce consumption or even move to another official tier. The smoker may simply switch to a slightly cheaper cigarette within the same tier.
This flexibility weakens the intended effect of tobacco taxation.
Cheap cigarettes remain widely available
Bangladesh already faces a major tobacco-use burden. According to the Global Adult Tobacco Survey 2017, 35.3% of adults used tobacco, while 18% smoked tobacco.
At the same time, cigarettes remain remarkably affordable. The WHO Report on the Global Tobacco Epidemic 2025 placed Bangladesh 163rd among 186 countries in terms of the price of the cheapest cigarette brand in 2024. In other words, Bangladesh remains among the countries where cheap cigarettes are most readily available.
The country also scored only 1.38 out of 5 in the fourth edition of the Cigarette Tax Scorecard, published in 2025. One reason for this poor performance is Bangladesh’s complex, multi-tiered ad valorem tax structure.
Under an ad valorem system, taxes are calculated as a percentage of the declared retail price. When numerous price points are available, cigarette companies can maintain cheaper brands and position products strategically across the market. Smokers who are sensitive to price can then switch brands rather than quit.
This is particularly concerning in a country where household incomes are limited and young people can access inexpensive cigarettes. The continued availability of very cheap brands undermines both public-health objectives and the effectiveness of tax increases.
Tax increases alone are not enough
Tobacco taxation is one of the most effective tools available for reducing tobacco consumption. But its effectiveness depends on more than the rate of tax.
The structure of the tax system matters just as much.
If taxes increase but cheaper alternatives remain widely available, many smokers will simply move down the price spectrum. This is known as down-trading. The more price points the market offers, the easier down-trading becomes.
The PROGGA survey provides a snapshot of how this mechanism operates in Bangladesh. With 53 brands spread across 12 price points, the cigarette market provides consumers with numerous alternatives at different levels of affordability.
As a result, a tax increase affecting one brand or price segment may not produce the expected reduction in cigarette consumption. It may merely redistribute smokers among brands.
A tax policy that raises the price of some cigarettes while leaving cheaper alternatives easily accessible cannot deliver its full public-health benefit.
Three reforms Bangladesh should pursue
The findings point to three urgent policy priorities.
First, the government should remove the phrase “and above” from cigarette price-tier definitions. As long as broad price ranges remain within each tier, manufacturers will be able to market cigarettes at multiple price points. Each tier should instead have a clearly specified retail price.
Second, Bangladesh should progressively reduce the number of cigarette price tiers, with the ultimate objective of introducing a single tier. A single price and tax tier would sharply reduce the opportunity to switch between cheaper and more expensive cigarettes.
Third, the country should move towards a simple, uniform specific excise tax. Under such a system, a fixed amount of tax would apply to each cigarette or pack, regardless of its retail price. The tax should be increased regularly so that cigarette prices rise faster than inflation and income growth.
This is essential because a nominal price increase does not automatically make cigarettes less affordable. If people’s incomes rise faster than cigarette prices, cigarettes may become more affordable over time, even after-tax increases.
Make all cigarettes less affordable
The objective of tobacco taxation should not be merely to make selected cigarette brands more expensive. It should be to make all cigarettes progressively less affordable and to leave consumers with fewer opportunities to avoid the intended impact of tax increases.
Bangladesh’s current system falls short of that objective.
Four official price tiers have produced at least 12 effective price points. The result is a market in which smokers can adjust their brand choices according to their ability to pay, instead of reducing consumption or quitting.
This is not simply a technical problem in tax administration. It is a public-health concern with consequences for families, healthcare expenditure and the country’s broader development.
Closing the price gaps, reducing the number of tiers and adopting a uniform specific tax would make the cigarette tax system simpler, more transparent and more effective. Most importantly, these reforms would help ensure that future tax increases lead to lower cigarette consumption rather than another round of brand switching.
ABM Zubair is Executive Director of PROGGA (Knowledge for Progress) and Director of the Centre for Research and Advocacy to Fight Tobacco (CRAFT), Bangladesh. Email: progga.bd@gmail.com .

PM seeks Japan’s proactive role in Bangladesh’s industrialisation, economic and technological advancement
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Tuesday, called on the Japanese government and private sector to play a more active role in Bangladesh’s economic development, technological advancement and industrialisation.

He made the call during a bilateral summit with his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi at the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office, Kantei, where they discussed expanding cooperation in key sectors, including energy, infrastructure, information and communication technology (ICT), trade and investment.

Tarique Rahman said Bangladesh was working to establish itself as a hub for economic activity, technology and manufacturing, highlighting the country’s growth potential and the opportunities for deeper engagement with Japanese businesses.

He noted that Bangladesh could become the world’s ninth-largest consumer economy by 2030, while its gross domestic product (GDP) could exceed one US dollar trillion by 2034.

In the meeting, they also discussed a plan to attract private investment worth one trillion Japanese yen (US$6.3 billion) in Bangladesh’s energy, infrastructure and ICT sectors and sending a Japanese team to Bangladesh soon to expedite the implementation of the proposed investment plan.

On energy security, Tarique Rahman said reliable and affordable energy supplies were essential to sustaining Bangladesh’s economic growth.

Expressing gratitude for Japan’s long standing support, he referred to the recent emergency assistance loan of 50 billion Japanese yen under the Partnership for Power Asia initiative to strengthen energy security in Asia.

He called for greater Japanese investment and participation in Bangladesh’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure, efficient power generation and renewable energy sectors.

To advance a technology-driven economy, the Prime Minister proposed establishing a Bangladesh-Japan Tech Park to connect Japanese companies, universities and investors with Bangladesh’s young talent, entrepreneurs and skilled technology professionals.

He said the proposed facility could prioritise artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, robotics and electronics manufacturing, creating opportunities for technology transfer, innovation and skilled employment.

Tarique Rahman also expressed interest in expanding cooperation in space science, satellite engineering and related technologies, drawing on Japan’s advanced capabilities in these fields.

Highlighting the need for modern and integrated transport infrastructure, he outlined plans for a high-speed railway network connecting Bangladesh’s six major divisional cities and a nationwide elevated-road network.

He sought Japanese technical assistance, investment and financing for planning and implementing such large-scale projects, saying Japan’s experience in infrastructure development and modern transport systems could help Bangladesh realise its development ambitions.

Welcoming fresh investment by Japanese businesses, the Prime Minister said his government was committed to improving the investment climate through greater transparency, predictability and efficiency in regulatory systems, tax policies, customs clearance and fund transfers.

He also expressed the hope that the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) would be implemented promptly.

“We need to work together to ensure that the benefits of the Economic Partnership Agreement reach the peoples of both countries,” he said.

Recalling the longstanding friendship between the two countries, the Prime Minister said Japan held a special place in the hearts of the people of Bangladesh.

Japan was among the earliest countries to recognise Bangladesh after its independence in 1971 and had remained one of its most valued development partners, contributing significantly to socioeconomic progress and infrastructure development.

He also recalled his father, Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman’s two visits to Japan and his mother, former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia’s contributions to strengthening bilateral ties, expressing his commitment to taking the partnership to new heights. On regional and international issues, Tarique Rahman reaffirmed the two countries’ shared commitment to multilateralism, international peace and respect for international law.

He thanked Japan for supporting Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman’s election as president of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) and expressed the hope of working closely with Tokyo to strengthen multilateral cooperation and address global challenges.

Reiterating the shared vision of a free, open, peaceful and inclusive Indo-Pacific, he stressed the importance of stronger regional connectivity, the free flow of trade and sustained economic growth.

Expressing deep concern over the deteriorating situation in Myanmar and the resulting Rohingya displacement crisis, the prime minister called for an end to all forms of violence, unhindered humanitarian assistance and dialogue among all concerned parties.

He appreciated Japan’s support for Bangladesh’s humanitarian efforts to shelter Rohingyas forcibly displaced from Myanmar’s Rakhine State and urged Tokyo to remain actively engaged with all parties to promote peace and stability in the region.

“A lasting solution to the Rohingya crisis lies in Myanmar,” he said, stressing the need for the early repatriation of the displaced people to their homeland in a voluntary, safe and dignified manner.

In his concluding remarks, Tarique Rahman expressed optimism that the summit would open a new chapter in Bangladesh-Japan relations, built on deeper trust, broader economic cooperation, stronger investment ties and a shared commitment to peace, stability and prosperity.

He proposed establishing a joint ministerial commission to identify priority areas, accelerate implementation and translate opportunities for cooperation into concrete initiatives. He also underscored the importance of closer engagement between the business communities of the two countries.

The Prime Minister invited Takaichi to visit Bangladesh at a mutually convenient time, expressing confidence that the longstanding friendship between the two countries would continue to deepen through mutual trust, cooperation and shared prosperity.

Following the summit, the two leaders made a joint press announcement on the outcomes of their discussions and exchanged several memorandums of understanding in key areas. Takaichi also hosted an official luncheon in honour of Tarique Rahman at the Kantei, the prime minister’s office.

The Bangladesh premier arrived in Tokyo on Monday for a four-day official visit at the invitation of Takaichi. During the visit, he is also scheduled to deliver the keynote address at the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum and meet Japanese business leaders.

item.title: Measles vaccine not working effectively
item.description:
A study has found that 27 per cent of children did not develop immunity (antibodies) against measles even after receiving the vaccine. This lack of immunity was more common among children aged 9 to 14 months.

Public health experts say the measles vaccine is not working effectively enough and that the government needs to rethink its approach to vaccination and the immunisation system.

The researchers involved said this was the first study of its kind to assess measles immunity among children under five in Bangladesh following the national measles-rubella vaccination campaign.

Twelve researchers and officials from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), the Directorate General of Drug Administration (DGDA), the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), the Institute of Public Health, the Eastern Mediterranean Public Health Network and Dhaka Homoeopathic Medical College conducted the study. The IEDCR led the research. Prothom Alo obtained a summary of the findings from a source familiar with the study.

Following a measles outbreak in March this year, the health authorities launched a nationwide measles-rubella vaccination campaign on 20 April. The authorities decided to vaccinate all children aged between six months and five years.

The campaign ended on 20 May. Before the campaign, senior health officials had said in April that infections would come under control within three to four weeks of its conclusion. However, measles transmission has continued even five months after the campaign ended.

Against this backdrop, people have raised questions about how effectively the measles vaccine develops immunity in children and whether the vaccine is working properly, given that infections remain uncontrolled. Public health experts have also repeatedly called for a study to assess the vaccine’s effectiveness.

Tajul A Bari, vaccine specialist Several factors can impair or reduce a vaccine’s effectiveness. Vaccines must be stored and transported at specific temperatures. This is a lengthy process, and temperatures may fluctuate at any stage. Such fluctuations can compromise the quality of the vaccine.

Findings of the study

The IEDCR-led study took place in September this year, following the conclusion of the national measles-rubella vaccination campaign. Researchers included 309 children from six suburban and rural areas across Dhaka, Mymensingh and Munshiganj districts.

The children were aged between 9 and 59 months. Researchers verified their vaccination status by checking vaccination cards and speaking to their guardians. They tested blood samples from the children at the IEDCR laboratory.

The researchers found that 203 of the 309 children, or 65.7 per cent, had developed measles antibodies. Another 21 children, or 6.8 per cent, had antibody levels within the borderline range.

A scientist from a government institution in the health sector, who spoke to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said, “We cannot say that these 21 children have developed antibodies, nor can we say that they have not.”

The study also found that 85 of the 309 children had developed no antibodies. In other words, 27.5 per cent of the children had not developed measles antibodies despite receiving the vaccine. The study found a higher prevalence of immunity among children aged 15 to 59 months than among those aged 9 to 14 months.

The researchers said that two or three doses of the vaccine produce stronger immunity than a single dose. However, the level of immunity among the children appears to be far below what is needed to stop measles transmission and prevent the disease from spreading.

Where do the risks lie?

Discussions with vaccine specialists and public health experts indicate that a vaccine’s effectiveness is partly related to a child’s age. If a child receives the vaccine at six months, 50 out of every 100 children will develop immunity.

At nine months, 85 out of every 100 children will develop immunity. If children receive the vaccine at 12 months, 90 per cent will develop immunity.

However, the IEDCR-led study found a much lower proportion of children who had developed immunity. Why did this happen?

Sources familiar with vaccination said that all vaccines used under the Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) have approval from the World Health Organization (WHO).

However, authorities do not test the quality of these vaccines, as no system exists for such testing. They simply assume that the vaccines meet the required quality standards.

Vaccine specialist Tajul A Bari told Prothom Alo, “Several factors can impair or reduce a vaccine’s effectiveness. Vaccines must be stored and transported at specific temperatures. This is a lengthy process, and temperatures may fluctuate at any stage. Such fluctuations can compromise the quality of the vaccine.”

Tajul A Bari added that vaccines may be less effective in children suffering from severe malnutrition. By contrast, the measles vaccine works better in children who receive breast milk. He said, “It is essential to investigate the exact reasons why the vaccine is not working effectively.”

The researchers found that 203 of the 309 children, or 65.7 per cent, had developed measles antibodies. Another 21 children, or 6.8 per cent, had antibody levels within the borderline range.

A complex situation

A joint independent review team comprising 70 local and international experts outlined the causes of the measles outbreak in Bangladesh at an event held at the Sonargaon Hotel in the capital on 14 October.

The team said structural weaknesses in the EPI leave around 20 per cent of children without routine vaccinations every year.

At the event, Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain said that authorities should not take a complacent approach to vaccines. Children must receive vaccines of assured quality.

Vaccines travel through several stages, from production to airports and other points along the supply chain, before finally reaching children. He stressed the need to ensure that vaccines retain their effectiveness throughout this process. He also sought cooperation from the World Health Organization, UNICEF, Gavi and other organisations represented at the event.

The IEDCR study has now found that 27 per cent of children failed to develop immunity despite receiving the measles vaccine. This means that a large number of children remain at risk of contracting measles. As these children grow older, they may pass beyond the age covered by the vaccination programme.

Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Hossain told Prothom Alo on Monday, “There is no reason to question the quality of the vaccine, as many countries are using it.”

Commenting on the IEDCR-led study, he said, “This is a very small study with a limited sample size. We should not draw any definitive conclusions from its findings. A larger study is needed.”

SMA Shafi, director of the Institute of Public Health, said researchers were conducting a more extensive study to assess and understand the situation. He told Prothom Alo that the study involved samples from 3,000 children, with researchers collecting samples from 100 children in each of 30 upazilas. They will publish the findings in the last week of November.

Measles deaths continue

According to a press release issued yesterday, Monday, by the Directorate General of Health Services’ Coordination and Control Centre, 1,388 people across the country sought hospital treatment for measles symptoms in the preceding 24 hours. Six people died with measles symptoms during the same period.

This year, 222,552 people have sought treatment for measles symptoms at public and private hospitals across the country. Measles has claimed 1,233 lives this year. Of these, 1,129 people died with measles symptoms, while authorities confirmed 104 deaths from measles.

Professor Be-Nazir Ahmed, a former director of the disease control branch of the government, said vaccination coverage must exceed 95 per cent under the current circumstances.

He told Prothom Alo, “We can see that the measles vaccine is not working effectively enough. We must also expand the eligible age range for vaccination and bring children over five years old under the programme. Eventually, we should extend it to people up to 18 years of age. We must ensure a national vaccination campaign every four years. Bangladesh will not be able to overcome this serious measles situation without a comprehensive plan.”

item.title: Why the IGP’s mention of ‘crossfire’ is alarming
item.description:
Every few days, we are reminded that our government, political parties, and institutions have learned nothing from past experience and remain incapable of abandoning their desire to repeat past mistakes. Our authorities repeatedly make it clear that they have no interest in making this state and its institutions citizen-centric. The recent remarks by the Inspector General of Police (IGP) provide ample reason for citizens to feel alarmed and for memories of past state violence to resurface.

On Monday, at the inauguration ceremony of the ‘Community Islamic Banking System’ in the capital’s Chawkbazar, IGP Md. Ali Hossain Fakir stated, “If crossfire is necessary, and if the government allows it, we will do just that. Accept that the police are needed from the cradle to the grave, and let me discharge my duties according to the law and the constitution.”

Debating whether police are necessary in society and the state is entirely pointless here. When we discuss that police must not violate human rights, steering that conversation towards the ‘necessity’ of the police serves only to sidestep our primary concern.

The ongoing discussion within civil society has never been about whether police are needed “from the cradle to the grave”; rather, it concerns how the police force exercises this role. The central question is whether they will construct a protective shield for citizens or become a lethal threat to them.

This brings us to our primary apprehension—crossfire. Since 2004, the question of how illegal, unconstitutional, or grave a human rights violation ‘crossfire’ or extrajudicial killing is has never truly been open to debate. From the outset, nearly all global human rights organisations have opposed and repeatedly condemned these practices. International bodies have even recommended banning RAB (which has now been dissolved and reconstituted as SRB) due to its involvement in extrajudicial killings.

In other words, as an institution, they do not even consider extrajudicial killings to be a “crime”. It is evident from the IGP’s statement that crossfire or extrajudicial killing is excluded from what they choose to classify as a crime.

Furthermore, the protests and resistance against such acts over the last decade and a half under the Awami League regime established a clear national consensus: the state cannot take a person’s life without due judicial process. Indeed, the right to life was one of the central demands of the July Uprising.

The IGP’s assertion that the police can execute crossfire if the government permits is, firstly, insulting to the country’s citizens. When an official paid by taxpayers’ money and sworn to serve the public expresses a desire to extrajudicially kill citizens, the reader can easily fathom how unconstitutional, humiliating, and terrifying that is.

Secondly, can he take a citizen’s life simply because the government desires it? Even if any law or constitutional provision were to grant permission to kill citizens in such a manner, why should citizens accept it?

Article 32 of the Constitution explicitly states, “No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty save in accordance with law.” Nevertheless, certain loopholes persist in the phrasing of the constitution and the penal code, allowing state forces to attempt to ‘legitimise’ any extrajudicial killing. This explains why the language and logical structure of official press notes following extrajudicial killings remain identical under every regime.

This brings us to the second and most vital question—if a member of a state force commits an extrajudicial killing or a similar human rights violation, who investigates it? The IGP claimed that they possess internal “checks and balances”. In his words, “If one of our members commits an offence and we fail to take action, only then can you accuse us of failing to act against them.”

This brings us to the second and most vital question—if a member of a state force commits an extrajudicial killing or a similar human rights violation, who investigates it?

The IGP implies that action is taken whenever police personnel commit a crime. However, this assertion cannot be applied to instances of crossfire. While RAB’s name has been consistently associated with crossfire, the police force has also been deeply involved.

According to a report by the Centre for Governance Studies, between 2019 and 2021, the involvement of police forces, including the Detective Branch (DB), in extrajudicial killings stood at 48.05 per cent, exceeding RAB’s involvement of 31.9 per cent.

We have also seen evidence that crossfire incidents are not merely isolated “crimes” by individuals, but are systemic in nature. For instance, Pradip Kumar Das, the former Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Teknaf police station, was awarded the ‘Bangladesh Police Medal’ (BPM), the highest honour in the police force, in 2019 for encounters. All six outstanding achievements he cited to police headquarters to secure the award involved the death of suspects (Prothom Alo, 6 August 2020). In other words, as an institution, they do not even consider extrajudicial killings to be a “crime”. It is evident from the IGP’s statement that crossfire or extrajudicial killing is excluded from what they choose to classify as a crime.

If this is the stance of a force chief, the question of who investigates human rights violations becomes critical once again. It has been proven once more that they are fundamentally incapable of investigating events that their own chief does not view as crimes—and which he expresses a willingness to carry out if the government so desires.

Following immediate criticism of the police chief’s remarks, police headquarters issued a clarification yesterday, Monday. The explanation regarding the right to self-defence contained both the traditional phrasing of post-crossfire official press releases and a veiled warning. It served as a reminder that the police can take such actions under the guise of the “law” for self-defence.

Such statements from the head of a state force openly expose their mindset towards citizens. In many countries across the world, even when protests turn violent, police firing rarely results in fatalities. Yet here, our police chief publicly voices an interest for extrajudicial killings!

This remark proves that a colonial mindset remains deeply entrenched within the psychology and administrative structure of the force. In the wake of the mass uprising, a golden opportunity arose to fundamentally reform the police force into a citizen-friendly, service-oriented institution. Have we carelessly squandered it?

At a time when ensuring the protection of citizens’ lives and liberties ought to be the primary priority in post-uprising Bangladesh, we are instead forced to hear veiled threats of state-sanctioned violence coming directly from the highest office of a law enforcement agency.

item.title: India braces for Cyclone Arnab with evacuations
item.description:
ANI_20260926401

Indian authorities ordered evacuations in southwestern Andhra Pradesh ahead of a severe cyclone expected to make landfall by Wednesday, the national weather office said.

Cyclone Arnab is forecast to hit the coast as a “very severe cyclonic storm”, with gusts of up to 140 kilometres (87 miles) per hour, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said in a bulletin on Tuesday.

Cyclones, called hurricanes in the North Atlantic and typhoons in the Pacific, are a regular menace in the Bay of Bengal and northern Indian Ocean.

The storm season, however, has been turbocharged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has caused unprecedented warming.

Neighbouring Sri Lanka, meanwhile, closed schools with warnings of torrential rain, with the island’s Department of Meteorology warning storms could trigger flash floods and mudslides.

The military has been placed on alert, Colombo’s Disaster Management Centre said.

India’s weather bureau said it expects the cyclone to result in “total destruction” of thatched houses and create localised flooding, uprooting of power and communication poles, and “widespread damage” to standing crops.

State Chief Minister Nara Chandrababu Naidu has ordered the storm be “constantly monitored and advance precautions taken”, his office said in a statement on Monday.

Local media reported that Andhra Pradesh authorities had ordered evacuations in key, low-lying areas and shut “all educational institutions” in some districts from Tuesday until Saturday.

Over 4,700 pregnant women residing in potentially dangerous localities were moved to hospitals, according to The Indian Express newspaper.

item.title: ‘They do not understand the language, cannot get lawyers, and their bodies are never returned’
item.description:
Death penalty for expatriates in saudi arabia: ‘They do not understand the language, cannot get lawyers, and their bodies are never returned’

The execution of foreign nationals is rising at an alarming rate in Saudi Arabia, with two Bangladeshis among those recently executed. In the first six months of this year alone, the country executed 59 foreign nationals. The imposition of the death penalty, particularly for drug-related offences, the transparency of judicial proceedings involving foreign defendants, allegations of torture and the limited opportunities to defend themselves have raised questions around the world. Against this backdrop, this is the final instalment of the series on Saudi Arabia’s judicial system and the way the death penalty is imposed.

One day in May last year, an Ethiopian prisoner was executed in Saudi Arabia. Before his execution, he called his mother back home and told her that he would be taken away the following morning. That would be his last breath. Hearing this, his mother burst into tears.

But the story did not end there. The Ethiopian man was executed, yet weeks passed without his body being returned to his family. Meanwhile, as his mother waited desperately for one last chance to see her son, she began showing signs of severe psychological distress. Eventually, she had to be admitted to a hospital’s psychiatric ward.

The incident was reported to London-based international human rights organisation Amnesty International by a member of the Ethiopian community. His own brother was also awaiting execution in Saudi Arabia. He said, “They [the Saudi rulers] are not just killing our brothers; they are killing us too.”

It is worth noting that 58 Ethiopians are currently being held in Khamis Mushait Prison in Saudi Arabia, facing the death penalty.

The heartbreaking case of the Ethiopian prisoner is not an isolated incident. A look at Saudi Arabia’s execution figures reveals a striking number of foreign nationals. Of the country’s total population of 35.3 million, around 44 per cent—approximately 15.7 million people—are foreign nationals or expatriates. Yet, between January 2014 and June 2025, Saudi Arabia executed 597 people for drug-related offences alone, nearly 75 per cent of whom were foreign nationals, according to Amnesty International.

According to data from the Berlin-based international human rights organisation European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR), of the 108 people executed in the first six months of this year (January–June), 59—or approximately 54 per cent—were foreign nationals. During the same period, 49 of the 71 executions carried out for drug-related offences involved foreign nationals.

How many were from each country?

The picture becomes clearer when the figures are examined more closely. According to Amnesty International, over the past decade, in addition to 150 Saudi nationals, those executed solely for drug-related offences included 155 Pakistanis, 66 Syrians, 50 Jordanians, 39 Yemenis, 33 Egyptians, 32 Nigerians, 22 Somalis and 13 Ethiopians.

Nationals of Iran, Afghanistan, Chad, Bahrain, Lebanon, Sudan, Türkiye, India and Palestine have also been executed. In other words, during this period, the number of Pakistani nationals executed exceeded the number of Saudi nationals.

However, these figures have limitations, as Amnesty International acknowledges. Its analysis is based solely on executions publicly announced by the Saudi authorities through the official news agency; the actual number is higher. The data do not capture whether discrimination occurs at every stage, from arrest and investigation to trial and sentencing.

The organisation also does not have access to official statistics on offences, arrests, charges or sentences. For these reasons, Amnesty International has called for an independent and transparent investigation into discrimination in the imposition of the death penalty on foreign nationals.

Death penalty in Saudi Arabia: What does the law say, and what happens in court?

Risks begin long before trial

The vulnerability of these expatriates begins long before they reach the courtroom—starting when they leave their home countries. Migrant workers make up approximately 77 per cent of Saudi Arabia’s total workforce.

According to Amnesty International’s analysis, their difficulties begin in their home countries, where they encounter fraudulent recruitment practices, and continue after they arrive in Saudi Arabia under the kafala, or sponsorship, system.

Kafala is a restrictive and exploitative migration system that places particular pressure on, and has a disproportionately negative impact on, migrant workers from African and Asian countries.

According to the guidelines of the International Organization for Migration (IOM), recruiting, transporting or harbouring a person for the purpose of exploitation through threats, force, coercion or deception falls within the definition of human trafficking. Such exploitation includes both forced labour and compelling people to engage in illegal activities.

The IOM has identified several factors that place expatriates in Saudi Arabia at risk. These include irregular migration; work hidden from public view, such as domestic work, maritime labour and employment in the informal sector; improper control by employers; corruption in recruitment; dependence on third-party brokers; and gaps in state protection.

These risks are not merely theoretical. In two cases documented by Amnesty International, the accused said they had been forced to transport prohibited drugs. However, the courts neither investigated nor accepted their accounts of the circumstances.

Bangladesh asks Saudi Arabia 6 questions over execution of 2 citizens

The organisation’s documented findings indicate that migrant workers in Saudi Arabia have been deceived by recruitment agents, forced to work excessive hours and subjected to wage theft. In some cases, these practices may amount to human trafficking for the purpose of labour exploitation.

United Nations human rights experts have also said that the impact of the death penalty falls disproportionately on foreign nationals. They have called for an end to this unequal impact on socially and economically disadvantaged groups, as these people are often unable to secure effective legal protection during trial and appeals.

Moreover, when someone experiences discrimination on multiple grounds at the same time, these disadvantages can intensify one another. For example, a person may face various difficulties simply because they are a migrant.

But if that person also belongs to a particular ethnic group and is a woman, obtaining legal assistance, asserting workplace rights or avoiding discrimination can become two or three times more difficult. In other words, rather than reducing one another, these disadvantages compound and multiply.

Alone in court, unable to understand the language

To understand how these vulnerabilities manifest in court, Amnesty International, with support from ESOHR and JPP (Justice Project Pakistan), documented 25 cases involving foreign nationals from Egypt, Ethiopia, Jordan, Pakistan and Somalia. All had been convicted of drug-related offences; some were awaiting execution, while others had already been executed.

Amnesty examined how the prisoners and their families navigated the Saudi judicial system, from arrest through sentencing and, in some cases, even after the executions.

Interviews were conducted with 13 family members, four members of the prisoners’ respective communities and one consular official. The organisation also reviewed court records relating to 15 other individuals.

The findings show that these people suffer a double disadvantage because of their limited education, language skills and financial resources. First, they face difficulties during migration. With little money and limited understanding of their rights and the relevant rules, they become vulnerable to fraud and exploitation by brokers from the very beginning of their journey to Saudi Arabia.

Second, once in Saudi Arabia, if they become involved in a legal dispute or criminal case, their limited financial means and education prevent them from hiring good lawyers or mounting an effective defence. In most cases, their opportunities to obtain consular assistance are also reduced. As a result, securing the right to a fair trial becomes difficult.

Many of the 25 individuals navigated the judicial system alone. They could not understand the court documents or the charges brought against them, and in some cases they were not even given copies of those documents. They received no consular assistance. Their unfamiliarity with Saudi Arabia’s criminal justice system, culture and language; their limited knowledge of their rights at the time of arrest; the risk of confessions being obtained without adequate interpretation or legal representation; and the lack of support—all combined to make it extremely difficult, and in some cases impossible, for them to navigate complex legal proceedings and mount an effective defence.

Rights are documented on paper.  Saudi Arabia’s 2013 Law of Criminal Procedure grants defendants the right to legal assistance during both investigation and trial, and prohibits torture.

However, the situation documented by ESOHR in cases involving prisoners facing the death penalty in Khamis Mushait, Najran and Tabuk prisons tells a different story. They have no professional interpreters or legal assistance, do not understand the judicial proceedings and have no effective opportunity to defend themselves. In many cases, prisoners did not even know when their sentences had been upheld or when their requests for clemency had been rejected.

Moved together, then taken away one by one...

In December 2024, United Nations human rights experts expressed grave concern over the imminent executions of three Egyptians. All three were executed on 3 December. They were part of a large group of at least 40 Egyptians awaiting execution in Tabuk Prison.

In November that year, the three Egyptians were moved, along with several other prisoners from Arab, African and Asian countries, including South Asia, to a separate ward. There, they witnessed fellow prisoners being taken away one by one for execution.

The other prisoners lived in fear of their own turn. According to Amnesty International, since 2024, 23 of those Egyptians have been executed, while 19 remain at risk of execution.

In November, two United Nations special rapporteurs also sent a joint letter to the Saudi government raising the issue of the three Egyptians and 29 other foreign men facing execution.

Of those 29 men, 28 were Egyptian and one was Jordanian. According to the latest information from ESOHR, eight Egyptians are currently being held in Tabuk Prison facing the death penalty.

The practice of moving foreign prisoners convicted of similar offences to separate wards together—as happened to Egyptians in Tabuk and Ethiopians and Somalis in Najran—is viewed by prisoners and their families as a grim indication that executions are imminent.

Prisoners interviewed by ESOHR also said they live in constant fear of execution. The United Nations and various experts have repeatedly condemned the practice of failing to provide advance notice of impending executions. In their view, this constitutes a form of ill-treatment that violates the absolute prohibition on torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.

“Your Turn Has Come”: A lifetime of uncertainty and fear

Families of prisoners often have no idea when an execution will take place. Amnesty International says Saudi law contains no clear provision requiring advance notice to be given to prisoners or their families. At most, family members have said, prisoners may be able to call home and inform them as little as 24 hours before an execution.

 In some cases, prison officials have informed prisoners the previous day, saying, “Your turn has come.” Many prisoners have told their families how fellow inmates were taken from their cells in the middle of the night, without any warning.

Other families learned of an execution through phone calls from fellow prisoners or through the media, after Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Interior announced it through the state news agency. In the case of one Pakistani prisoner, his family learned of the execution several days later through phone calls from others who were awaiting execution.

In some cases, prison officials themselves asked prisoners to convey the news. Because of the distance and infrequent phone contact, such families can spend years living with uncertainty.

For families whose loved ones have spent years awaiting execution, the lack of transparency about the progress of their cases, irregular communication and the constant fear of execution combine to create a state of “lifelong anxiety and despair”.

The financial burden adds to their suffering: following an arrest, the family loses its primary breadwinner. They must also endure the pain of watching their loved one’s physical and mental condition deteriorate from afar.

Bodies never returned

For some families, the suffering is compounded by the withholding of their loved ones’ bodies. Saudi law does not guarantee that remains will be handed over to families.

Three of the 25 individuals documented by Amnesty International were executed between January and June 2025. In all three cases, Saudi Arabia did not return the bodies to their families or disclose where they had been buried. As a result, the families were deprived even of the fundamental right to mourn in accordance with their cultural and religious traditions, the organisation said.

For the family of Hussein Abu al-Khair, a Jordanian prisoner, the ordeal was even more complicated. When executions for drug-related offences were suspended, he received conflicting information about the status of his case. In March 2023, he was executed without any advance notice.

Upon hearing the news, his family in the capital, Amman, initially sat in silence before beginning to “scream like mad”, his sister said. She recalled, “We were devastated, especially because there was no body of our brother in front of us to mourn. There was no opportunity to hold a final farewell either.”

Concerns among Bangladeshi families

The situation surrounding judicial proceedings and the death penalty for expatriates in Saudi Arabia has a profound and direct impact on Bangladeshi families as well.

Bangladeshis make up the largest group of foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, numbering at least 2.5 million. They are followed by Indians, Pakistanis, Yemenis and Egyptians.

According to ESOHR, Bangladeshi nationals were among the 108 people executed in the first six months of 2026. More recently, two Bangladeshis convicted of “immoral acts” at a mosque in the holy city of Mecca were executed; they are not included in the figures for those six months. The number of Bangladeshis executed during that period is not known.

As noted earlier, Amnesty International documented 25 cases to examine in detail the discrimination and legal challenges faced by expatriates sentenced to death in Saudi courts and under the country’s judicial system. The cases involved prisoners from Egypt, Ethiopia, Jordan, Pakistan and Somalia.

Bangladesh was also absent from the list of nationalities mentioned by the organisation among those whose citizens had been executed for drug-related offences. This does not mean Bangladeshis are excluded from the figures, as their names appear on ESOHR’s list. Rather, the problem is a lack of information.

ESOHR has reported that it was unable to obtain or document any information before the executions in 91 of the 108 cases, or 84.2 per cent. Amnesty International also lacks official statistics on arrests, charges or sentences.
