As a result, there are no answers about the number of Bangladeshi prisoners, the nature of the charges against them, their access to lawyers and interpreters, or the consular assistance they receive.

Conclusion

In December 2024, the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination identified racial and ethnic discrimination in Saudi Arabia’s criminal justice system. The committee expressed concern that Shia minorities, migrant workers and domestic workers, including women, were being subjected to arbitrary detention, torture and ill-treatment.

The committee called on Saudi Arabia to impose a moratorium on executions and move towards abolishing the death penalty. Amnesty International has also called for an independent and transparent investigation into whether discrimination or bias occurs in the country’s judicial proceedings and the imposition of the death penalty.

Not understanding the language, being unable to obtain a lawyer, receiving the final news too late and never getting the body back—these stages are all links in the same chain.

According to Amnesty International, expatriates arrested or detained in Saudi Arabia face multiple complex and interconnected problems at the same time. They find themselves in an unfamiliar judicial system, cannot understand its language and culture, and have no one to provide legal assistance or interpretation. Taken together, these barriers make their struggle to prove their innocence or save their lives almost impossible.

At the far end of this chain is the Ethiopian mother mentioned at the beginning of this report, who heard her son speak of his “last breath”. After weeks passed without his body being returned, she eventually had to be admitted to a hospital’s psychiatric ward.

Sources

1.  World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), Law of Criminal Procedure (promulgated by Royal Decree No. M/39 of 28 Rajab 1422 [16 October 2001]), Saudi Arabia.

2.  Amnesty International, Saudi Arabia: “If We Had Money and a Lawyer, Maybe My Brother Would Be Alive”: Saudi Arabia’s Execution Crisis, 7 July 2025.

3.  Joint report by MENA Rights Group, ALQST for Human Rights and the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR), Death Penalty in Saudi Arabia: Joint Submission to the Special Rapporteur on Extrajudicial, Summary or Arbitrary Executions, 10 March 2026.

4.  ESOHR, 108 Saudi Arabia: Executions in the First Half of 2026.

item.title: Israel to give verdict on Netanyahu in pivotal election
item.description:
A deeply divided Israel heads to the polls on Tuesday for the first time since Hamas’s 7 October, 2023 attack, with voters delivering their verdict on veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the country’s rightward drift.

Israelis are casting their ballots in the shadow of three years of multi-front regional wars triggered by 7 October, with the trauma still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign.

The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by a devastating military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank, and a move towards hard-right religious nationalism.

The last polls to be published showed Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, running neck and neck with his main centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot, a political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent.

Some 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, with more than half a million young people due to cast their ballot for the first time. Surveys show they overwhelmingly identify as centre-right or right-wing.

Tens of thousands of Israelis are estimated to have flown in from abroad to vote in an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country.

“I think this is one of the most important election days in the history of the state of Israel,” Uriel Brandler, a 58-year-old real estate agent, told AFP in Jerusalem the day before the vote.

“The country definitely needs a change for the better in every aspect.”

Netanyahu, 77, has served as Israel’s prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.

The wily political operator focused heavily on his security credentials during his campaign, playing on his relationship with US President Donald Trump and insisting he is the only one who can keep Israelis safe.

In the years since 7 October, Netanyahu led multiple wars that have seen Israeli forces reduce Gaza to rubble, occupy southern Lebanon and for the first time pummel arch-foe Iran with US help.

At home, Israelis have faced bombardment from Iran, Hamas, Lebanese militant group Hezbollah, and Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

‘Not afraid to take action’

Zipporah Bennett, an 85-year-old retiree, said she was voting for Netanyahu “because he has had the experience of navigating the country through a lot of difficult seasons”.

“He has the full support of the American government,” she said, “and I believe he’s a man who’s not afraid to take action.”

Netanyahu returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket.

The opposition has scorned the premier for his backing of ultra-Orthodox parties fighting to keep exemptions for religious Jewish students from drafting into the military, which faces personnel shortages.

But one of the biggest criticisms levelled at Netanyahu is his failure to take responsibility for the 7 October attack, the deadliest day in the country’s history.

Eisenkot, 66, has pledged to establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the attack, something Netanyahu’s government has resisted.

Seeking to unseat the premier is an informal bloc of parties led by Eisenkot’s Yashar and spanning from the right to the centre-left.

Eisenkot has vowed to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state and expressed support for Israeli settlements, but has promised to crack down on violent settlers.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu have publicly said they would partner with the predominantly Arab lists, which represent some 21 percent of Israel’s population and who could become kingmakers if the results are as close as expected.

Most polling stations will close at 10:00 pm (2000 GMT).

Final results could take days to trickle in and it is highly unlikely that any single party will come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member parliament.

Cobbling together any coalition could take weeks or months, with possible new elections on the horizon if negotiations fail.

item.title: CPB activists attacked, party headquarters besieged
item.description:
Activists of the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB) brought out a procession after the release of Dipak Shil, former president of the Bangladesh Chhatra Union, who had been detained while attempting to hold a human chain in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, in protest against female Baul singers being prevented from performing in Sunamganj.

CPB activists were attacked in the capital’s Purana Paltan area over allegations that they had chanted the slogan ‘Joy Bangla’ during the procession.

CPB leaders said the attackers identified themselves as leaders and activists of Jubo Dal and Chhatra Dal, youth and student wings of ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) respectively.

The attack began at around 10:00 pm on Monday. For about an hour, the attackers remained in front of the CPB’s central office in Purana Paltan, chanting various slogans. They also beat two CPB activists. Police later arrived and rescued them.

When this correspondent visited the scene at around 11:30 pm, police were deployed in front of the CPB’s central office, while several party activists were standing nearby.

CPB leaders said that, following Dipak Shil’s release, the procession began in front of the party’s central office, with Shil accompanying the activists, and ended at Paltan intersection. A brief rally was then under way when the participants chanted ‘Joy Bangla, Joy Samajtantra (Socialism)’.

At that point, 40 to 50 people identifying themselves as Jubo Dal and Chhatra Dal activists objected to the use of the ‘Joy Bangla’ slogan. An argument broke out between the two groups.

At one stage, those identifying themselves as Jubo Dal and Chhatra Dal activists chanted, “Awami Leaguer Thikana, Ei Banglai Hobe Na (There is no place for the Awami League in this Bengal).” After the exchange continued for some time, they beat two CPB activists.

CPB activists further said that, after the assault, their colleagues returned from Paltan intersection to the front of the party’s central office. The two sides then chased each other for a while. The attackers subsequently took up positions in front of the CPB office with sticks and other wooden weapons, chanting various slogans. They left after 11:00 pm.

Jolly Talukder, a member of the CPB presidium, told Prothom Alo that the party had been attacked despite its role in the July mass uprising. “The government must rein in its own party members. How can they come and launch an attack in front of a political party’s office?” she said.

Talukder alleged that police had detained CPB members Iran Molla and Sohel Fakir following the attack. However, Ariful Alam, officer-in-charge of Paltan police station, denied that anyone had been detained.

He told Prothom Alo that 15 to 20 people had brought out a procession in the Paltan area following the release of former Bangladesh Chhatra Union president Dipak Shil.

“Some local people alleged that the slogan ‘Joy Bangla’ had been chanted during the procession. An argument subsequently broke out between them. There was no vandalism at the CPB office, and no one was detained,” he said.

Late at night, CPB’s former general secretary Ruhin Hossain said that police had released Iran Molla and Sohel Fakir.

Asked about the attack, Chhatra Dal’s central general secretary Nasir Uddin told Prothom Alo, “We are not aware of any incident in which Chhatra Dal leaders or activists went to the CPB office to stage a protest. Chhatra Dal has issued no instructions for any of its leaders or activists to do anything of this kind. We are looking into what actually happened.”

At around 12:15 am on Tuesday, CPB General Secretary Abdullah Kafi Ratan briefed journalists in front of the party’s central office.

“On 15 March 2025, an attempt was made to attack our party office after it had been announced in advance. Those who opposed the country’s independence during the Liberation War attempted that attack. They failed because we resisted them. We feel that, through tonight’s attack, they are trying to vent their frustration over that failure,” he said.

Referring to the CPB’s role in the July–August 2024 movement, Ratan said, “On 26 July 2024, we took to the streets of Dhaka in a procession, defying the curfew. On 2 August, we held the Droho Jatra (march of defiance). Yet today we are being branded as collaborators of fascists and the ousted government. Those making these allegations are trying to fish in troubled waters.”

The CPB general secretary recalled the party office had previously been attacked during the Ershad regime. On 5 May 2013, he said, the building had been set on fire with gunpowder up to the third floor. The party had been banned for 23 years during the Pakistan period, and Ziaur Rahman had also banned it in 1977. “Yet no one has been able to wipe out our party,” he said.

Speaking about the attackers, Ratan said, “They came to attack us late at night, but our comrades came from their respective areas and protected the party office. We are prepared to give our lives, but we will not tolerate any attack on the Communist Party.”

“We want to tell those who formed mobs to demolish shrines, burn newspaper offices and attack party offices that they cannot harm the Communist Party through mob violence,” he added.

Explaining what he believed might have prompted the attack, Ratan said, “One of our comrades had been arrested. His name is Dipak Shil, a former leader of the Bangladesh Chhatra Union. I have heard that a procession was held here after his release. The slogans ‘Joy Samajtantra’ and ‘Joy Sarbohara (Proletariat)’ were chanted during the procession. The attackers may have misinterpreted those slogans and used them as a pretext for the attack. But no slogan can justify an attack on a party office.”

Speaking on the slogan ‘Joy Bangla’, the CPB general secretary said, “‘Joy Bangla’ is a slogan of our Liberation War. The Awami League committed many wrongs while using the slogan ‘Joy Bangla’, but that does not mean we will abandon it. Even if someone chanted ‘Joy Bangla’ during our procession, that cannot be used as an excuse to attack the Communist Party’s office.”

Regarding the attackers’ identities, Ratan said, “Those who carried out the attack identified themselves as members of a particular party. We are not certain whether that claim is true. We have spoken to local leaders of the ruling party, who said the attackers were not members of their party.”

Ratan also said the party would review CCTV footage of the incident, gather the necessary information and provide further details at a news conference later.

item.title: When to file income tax returns to avoid penalties
item.description:
Taxpayers have only two months left to file their income tax returns without penalties. They can submit their returns and pay the applicable tax without any penalty until 31 December. Those who file their returns from 1 January onwards will face penalties.

From this year, the National Board of Revenue (NBR) has made online tax return submission mandatory for all taxpayers. The system will therefore calculate the applicable tax automatically.

As a result, if taxpayers try to submit their returns from 1 January onwards by paying only the assessed tax, the NBR system will not accept their submissions.

Bangladesh currently has more than 12.5 million holders of Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TINs). Of them, only around five million file their tax returns each year.

5 penalties for failing to file income tax return; includes disconnection of gas, electricity

When can you receive tax relief, when will you face penalties

Taxpayers who filed their returns in the first quarter of the current financial year (July–September) will receive a tax relief of 5 per cent of the tax paid or Tk 25,000, whichever is lower. However, the relief applies only to the tax paid at the time of filing the return.

Those filing their returns in the second quarter (October–December), including the current period, will not receive any tax relief. They only need to pay the applicable tax, with no incentives available.

Taxpayers who file their returns in the January–March quarter will have to pay an additional amount equivalent to 2 per cent of the tax payable or Tk 3,000, whichever is higher. The penalty will increase further for returns filed after March.

Those filing returns between April and June will have to pay an additional amount equivalent to 5 per cent of the tax payable or Tk 5,000, whichever is higher.

How to pay tax

Taxpayers can pay their taxes from home and submit their income tax returns online using bank transfers, debit cards, credit cards, bKash, Rocket, Nagad or other mobile financial service applications.

If taxpayers encounter any problems while filing their returns online, NBR officials will provide round-the-clock assistance through the call centre and other electronic channels to resolve them promptly.

Keep your documents safe

A taxpayer’s responsibility does not end with submitting a return. Taxpayers should preserve the necessary documents for the prescribed period so that they can readily produce them if tax officials conduct an audit in the future.

Submitting a return with incorrect or incomplete information can expose taxpayers to risks.

item.title: Karnaphuli Garden City in Dhaka closes, what led to its closure?
item.description:
Karnaphuli Garden City shopping complex opened in Kakrail, Dhaka, towards the end of the last century. At the time, the upscale shopping centre attracted middle- and upper-income shoppers looking for clothes, shoes, cosmetics, jewellery and various other products.

However, over the years, the complex gradually lost customers for several reasons. Sales fell so sharply that shop owners decided to close the entire shopping centre on 1 October.

During a visit to Karnaphuli Garden City shopping complex on Monday afternoon, the main entrance was found shuttered. A PVC banner hanging above it read, “The shopping complex will remain closed from 1 October.”

Although the main entrance was closed, six or seven shops on either side and an ATM booth remained open. Four or five customers were seen at two of the food outlets.

An inquiry revealed that Karnaphuli Garden City shopping complex opened in 1998, occupying the basement and four floors of a 20-storey building. The remaining floors housed apartments.

The Karnaphuli Group developed the complex, and 125 businesspeople purchased ownership rights to its 198 shops. With customers no longer visiting in sufficient numbers, the shop owners unanimously decided to close the complex and sell their ownership interests.

Leaders of the Karnaphuli Garden City Shop Owners’ Association said the complex initially housed shops selling ready-made garments, shoes, cosmetics, tailoring services, jewellery and various other products.

The fourth floor housed a food court. Although the complex had 198 shops, only 25 remained operational before its closure.

A visit to the shopping complex

On the left side of the complex are outlets of Kacchi Bhai, a very popular kacchi chain, and Hot Cake. A Raymond outlet stands on the other side.

Mohammad Mamun, an employee at the Raymond outlet, said, “Although the market has closed, the owner of our shop has not yet served us any notice. We will have to leave if the owner gives us notice.”

Jahidul Islam, owner of Gyan Bichitra, a coffee shop next to Raymond, said, “Business is not doing well because the market has closed. We will also vacate our shop next month.”

Meanwhile, Mizanur Rahman, manager of the Shumi’s Hot Cake outlet said, “Our shop owner has not told us anything yet. So, we are still unsure whether we will stay or leave.”

Asked about business at the complex, he said it had been without customers for a long time.

Why the shopping complex closed             

Bakibillah Osmani is the general secretary of the shop owners' association for Karnaphuli Garden City Shopping Complex, said sales at the complex had gradually declined for more than a decade.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said three or four main factors had left the shopping centre without customers. As a result, all the shop owners jointly decided to sell their ownership interests.

Osmani added that severe traffic congestion during the construction of the Moghbazar–Malibagh flyover over the past decade had significantly reduced the number of shoppers visiting the complex.

Several shop owners temporarily relocated their businesses to nearby markets. However, after construction of the flyover ended, they did not leave their new locations to return to the complex.

Later, the covid-19 pandemic dealt another blow, forcing more than 100 shops to close. Those shops never reopened. In addition, allegations that several cosmetics shops in the complex sold substandard products damaged its reputation.

“We have started discussions with hospitals, banks and corporate organisations about selling the market premises. We expect to finalise the sale soon,” the shop owners’ association leader said.

The Karnaphuli Group developed Karnaphuli Garden City shopping complex. Former Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Saber Hossain Chowdhury is associated with the group's ownership.

item.title: PM invites Japanese investors to join Bangladesh’s next growth phase
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Tuesday, invited Japanese investors, businesses and financial institutions to explore investment opportunities in Bangladesh and become partners in the country’s next phase of economic growth.

“The partnership between Bangladesh and Japan has been built on decades of friendship, trust, and mutual respect. Today, we have an opportunity to take this relationship to new heights. I warmly invite Japanese investors, businesses, and financial institutions to explore the opportunities Bangladesh has to offer and be part of our next phase of growth,” he said.

The prime minister made the call at a joint press announcement at the conference room of the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office (Kantei) here following his high-level bilateral talks with prime minister Sanae Takaichi.

Tarique Rahman said the two leaders had held fruitful discussions on a broad range of bilateral, regional and international issues, reaffirming their commitment to strengthening the longstanding partnership.

He said the two countries had expressed a shared commitment to enhancing cooperation in energy, information and communication technology (ICT), railways and infrastructure, deep-sea ports and foreign direct investment (FDI).

Tarique Rahman, Prime MinisterJapan holds a special place in the hearts of the people of Bangladesh. Our friendship is rooted in mutual respect, trust and a shared vision of peace, prosperity, and stability.

The prime minister said Bangladesh is committed to working with Japanese partners to unlock economic potential through productive investment, technology transfer, skilled employment and mutually beneficial business ventures.

“Together, we can build a more resilient and prosperous future for both our great nations,” he added.

During the visit, Bangladesh and Japan also exchanged several memorandums of understanding (MoUs) in key areas, he said, adding that a joint statement would outline the outcomes and shared priorities of their discussions.

Recalling Japan’s long standing role as a development partner, Tarique Rahman said, “Japan holds a special place in the hearts of the people of Bangladesh. Our friendship is rooted in mutual respect, trust and a shared vision of peace, prosperity, and stability.”

“Japan, a peace-loving nation, is one of the earliest countries’ to recognize Bangladesh following our independence in 1971,” he said.

The prime minister added, “For more than three decades, Japan has been one of our most valued development partners, making significant contributions to Bangladesh’s socio-economic progress and infrastructure development. We deeply appreciate this enduring friendship.”

Tarique Rahman expressed gratitude to Takaichi and the Japanese people for their warm welcome and hospitality during his official visit.

“Our ambition is clear: to turn this friendship between our two nations into a powerful engine of economic opportunity and shared prosperity,” he said, adding, “Together, let us build a partnership that serves our peoples today and creates a lasting legacy for generations to come.”

Earlier, Takaichi welcomed Tarique Rahman at the Kantei, where the Bangladesh prime minister was accorded a guard of honour before the two leaders held their summit meeting.

The two prime ministers also introduced members of their respective delegations to each other before proceeding to the talks.

Tarique Rahman arrived in Tokyo on Monday on a four-day official visit at the invitation of Takaichi. He was received at Narita International Airport by Japanese State Minister for Foreign Affairs Yasutaka Nakasone.

On the first day of the visit, Tarique Rahman held separate meetings with a high-level Japanese parliamentary delegation led by former prime minister Taro Aso, Marubeni Corporation Chairman Masumi Kakinoki and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) President Dr Akihiko Tanaka.

This is Tarique Rahman’s third state visit abroad since taking office on February 17 this year. He previously visited Malaysia and China and travelled to New York in September to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

item.title: Tarique-Takaichi talks begin in Tokyo as Bangladesh PM accorded warm welcome at Japanese PM’s Office
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Tuesday, began high-level bilateral talks with his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi at the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office here aimed at strengthening bilateral relations, expanding trade and investment, and enhancing cooperation between the two friendly countries.

The summit began at 11:40 am local time at the Kantei, the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office, with Tarique Rahman representing Bangladesh and Takaichi representing Japan.

The talks are expected to focus on strengthening bilateral relations, expanding trade and commercial activities, increasing Japanese cooperation in key sectors, and exchanging views on regional and international issues.

Earlier, Takaichi welcomed Tarique Rahman upon his arrival at the Kantei at 11:32 am. The two prime ministers stood side by side on a ceremonial platform as a contingent of Japan’s armed forces accorded the Bangladesh prime minister a guard of honour, accompanied by the national anthems of the two countries.

Tarique Rahman inspected the guard of honour before introducing members of his delegation to Takaichi. The Japanese prime minister, in turn, introduced members of her cabinet to the Bangladesh leader.

After the ceremonial proceedings, the Bangladesh prime minister signed the visitors’ book at the entrance to the main building before the two leaders proceeded to their summit meeting.

The talks are scheduled to continue until 12:10 pm, followed by a joint press announcement at 12:15 pm on the outcomes of their discussions.

Takaichi is scheduled to host a luncheon in honour of Tarique Rahman at the Kantei at 12:30 pm. At the beginning of the luncheon, she will deliver a brief welcome address. In response, Tarique Rahman will deliver his remarks.

Bangladesh and Japanese national flags were displayed along the road leading to the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office to welcome the Bangladesh prime minister.

The Bangladesh delegation includes Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, and Prime Minister’s Adviser on Posts, Telecommunications, ICT and Science and Technology Rehan Asif Asad.

The visit is expected to open new avenues for bilateral cooperation and attract fresh Japanese private investment in Bangladesh, Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam said at a curtain-raiser press conference back in Dhaka.

He said the two countries would focus on the effective implementation of the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market and strengthening business engagement.

The two sides are also expected to explore cooperation in renewable energy, agriculture, science and technology, digital transformation, skills development and human resource development.

Siam said several memorandums of understanding (MoUs) were under discussion for signing during the visit. The proposed agreements cover agriculture, fisheries, human resource and skills development, domestic aviation, trade, environmental conservation and the modernisation of local government.

During the four-day visit, Tarique Rahman is also scheduled to deliver the keynote address at the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum and meet Japanese business leaders.

The prime minister arrived in Tokyo Monday morning at the invitation of Takaichi. He was received at Narita International Airport by Japanese State Minister for Foreign Affairs Yasutaka Nakasone.

On the first day of the visit, Tarique Rahman held separate meetings with a high-level Japanese parliamentary delegation led by former prime minister Taro Aso, Marubeni Corporation Chairman Masumi Kakinoki and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) President Dr Akihiko Tanaka.

During his meeting with Aso, the Bangladesh prime minister recalled their meeting in Japan in 2006, acknowledged Aso’s contribution to strengthening bilateral relations and invited him to visit Bangladesh again, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said.

At the meeting with Kakinoki, discussions focused on expanding trade and investment, implementing the EPA and exploring Japanese investment in information and communication technology, energy and advanced manufacturing. Tarique Rahman also discussed modernising Karnaphuli Fertilizer Company Limited and exploring the possibility of establishing a second fertiliser factory.

During his meeting with JICA President Tanaka, the prime minister discussed continued Japanese support for infrastructure and economic development projects, faster implementation of ongoing projects and proposals for a Bangladesh-Japan Skills Partnership and a Technological Village and Innovation City.

Agricultural modernisation, agro-processing, light engineering and energy security also featured in the discussions.

Other members include Invest Bangladesh Authority Chairman Ashik Chowdhury, Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman, Prime Minister’s Special Assistant for Overseas Employment in the Asia-Pacific Region Dr Md Shakirul Islam Khan, Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam, Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury, Economic Relations Division Secretary Shahriar Kader Siddiky and Prime Minister’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon.

Hefazat-e-Islam Joint Secretary General and Nezame Islam Party acting Secretary General Azizul Hoque Islamabadi and Am Janata Dal General Secretary Md Tarek Rahman are also accompanying the prime minister.

This is Tarique Rahman’s third state visit abroad since taking office on February 17 this year. He previously visited Malaysia and China and travelled to New York in September to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

item.title: Caretaker govt: Complications over chief adviser’s appointment process
item.description:
There is no disagreement between the government and the opposition over restoring the caretaker government system for holding general elections. Political parties reached a consensus on the issue during discussions at the National Consensus Commission under the interim government. However, there is still a lack of clarity over how this government will be formed and through what process its chief adviser will be appointed.

The July Charter contains an agreement on selecting the chief adviser through a parliamentary selection committee. However, political differences remain on certain aspects of the selection process.

Against this backdrop, the Parliamentary Special Committee on Reformation of Constitution is now inviting proposals from stakeholders on what the framework of the caretaker government could look like. It has already received a new idea, although the framework has yet to be finalised. Questions have also been raised about how realistic the new idea is.

The opposition is not represented on the Special Committee on Reformation of Constitution. It does not want to be part of the process. People concerned said that the election-time government system has been one of the major causes of political crises in the country. If the framework for this government cannot be determined on the basis of consensus, there is a risk of another political crisis in the future.

Political disputes over the election-time government system have continued in the country for a long time. Although the 1991 national election was held under an interim caretaker government, the system had no constitutional basis. Following political movements, a non-party caretaker government system was incorporated into the Constitution in 1996. The system was abolished in 2011 through the 15th Amendment during the Awami League government. Last year, a verdict by the Appellate Division called for the reinstatement of the provisions relating to the caretaker government system.

The current government also supports restoring the system. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told journalists last Sunday that a political understanding had been reached to hold the next national parliamentary election under a caretaker government. He also said the government was committed to restoring the caretaker government system through a constitutional amendment.

What was the framework of the caretaker government?

The 13th Amendment incorporated provisions for a non-party caretaker government during elections into the Constitution. It stipulated that the last retired chief justice would serve as the chief adviser of the government. If the last retired chief justice was unavailable or declined to take responsibility, the chief justice who had retired immediately before him would be appointed as chief adviser. If no retired chief justice was available or willing to take the responsibility, the retired Appellate Division judge who had most recently retired would be invited to take the post.

If no retired judge of the Appellate Division was available or none of them agreed to become chief adviser, the president would appoint a person to the post after consulting the major political parties. If no one could be found through this process either, the president would assume the responsibility of chief adviser to the non-party caretaker government in addition to his own duties.

Controversy arose over the formation of the caretaker government in 2006. At the time, the opposition Awami League (now banned from activities in the country) alleged that the retirement age of judges had been raised to ensure that a preferred person could become the head of the caretaker government. The party launched a movement over the issue. On 28 October that year, five people were killed in clashes with Jamaat-e-Islami in the Baitul Mukarram area of the capital during the Awami League’s logi-baitha movement. Four of those killed were Jamaat activists and one was a Workers Party activist.

Amid the anarchy, President Iajuddin Ahmed took oath as the head of the caretaker government. The events eventually led to the 1/11 political changeover. On 11 January 2007, another caretaker government, led by Fakhruddin Ahmed, took oath.

Although there is political consensus on restoring the caretaker government system, strong opinions were expressed during discussions at the National Consensus Commission in favour of keeping the president and the judiciary out of the process. During consultations by the constitutional amendment committee, many stakeholders have also advised that the framework be determined without involving the judiciary and the president. This has raised a fresh question: Who will become the chief adviser, and how will a suitable person be selected for the post?

What the July Charter says

The July Charter outlines a detailed framework for the caretaker government system. It proposes that the chief adviser be selected through a parliamentary selection committee. After being appointed, the chief adviser will select up to 15 advisers in consultation with the selection committee.

All 30 political parties and alliances that took part in discussions at the National Consensus Commission, including the ruling BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) and the opposition Jamaat-e-Islami, agreed to the proposal. However, there were differences of opinion on certain aspects of the selection process.

The charter proposes that an election be held within 90 days after the expiry of the parliament’s term or its dissolution for any other reason. The appointment of the chief adviser to the election-time caretaker government must be finalised 15 days before the expiry of parliament’s term. If parliament is dissolved for any reason other than the expiry of its term, the appointment must be finalised within the following 15 days.

Where the differences over the process lie

The July Charter states that the selection committee will comprise the prime minister, the leader of the opposition, the speaker, the deputy speaker (from the opposition) and a representative of the second-largest opposition party in parliament.

Within 24 hours of the formation of the committee, it will seek the names of eligible candidates for the post of chief adviser from registered political parties, political parties represented in parliament and independent MPs. Each political party and each independent MP will be allowed to propose only one name. Political parties and independent MPs will submit their proposed names to the Parliament Secretariat within the following 24 hours. The committee may also search for names on its own initiative. Jamaat-e-Islami is in favour of using only political parties instead of registered political parties.

Within the next 72 hours, committee members will meet to discuss among themselves the names they have found through their own searches and those proposed by political parties and independent MPs. They will then select one person as the chief adviser of the caretaker government. The president will appoint that person as chief adviser.

If no candidate can be finalised through this process within 120 hours, the ruling party or alliance in parliament will propose five names, the main opposition party or alliance five names, and the second-largest opposition party in parliament two names for the post of chief adviser within the following 48 hours. The speaker will make the names public.

Within the next 48 hours, the main opposition party or alliance will select one person from the list proposed by the ruling party or alliance. Similarly, the ruling party will select one person from the list proposed by the main opposition. If the proposing parties reach a consensus on any one of the names selected through this process, that person will be nominated as the chief adviser of the next caretaker government. Alternatively, a candidate may be selected if four of the five members agree.

If this process also fails, two representatives of the judiciary will be added to the selection committee within the next 24 hours. However, they will not be allowed to propose any names. The seven-member committee will select a chief adviser through a ranked-choice voting system under the supervision of the speaker within the following 24 hours. The BNP, however, has a different opinion on this method. This is the main point of political disagreement over the proposal in the July Charter.

The July Charter states that if the chief adviser still cannot be appointed through these processes, the provisions of the 13th Amendment will have to be followed. However, the president cannot be selected as the head of the caretaker government in this case. The BNP, Jamaat and 26 other parties agreed to this proposal.

A new idea

A new idea emerged at a meeting of the special committee on constitutional reform last Saturday. It proposes that the upper house of parliament have a longer term than the lower house. Discussions have also taken place on whether the process of forming a caretaker government could involve the upper house.

In this case, if the post of vice-president is created, the vice-president could be made the speaker of the upper house. An alternative proposal is that the speaker of the upper house be elected with the consent of the ruling and opposition parties. The speaker would then head the caretaker government, while the other advisers would also be appointed from the upper house with the consent of both the ruling and opposition parties. The special committee made no decision on the matter at its meeting.

Badiul Alam Majumdar, a former member of the National Consensus Commission, told Prothom Alo that if the speaker of the upper house were made the head of the caretaker government, the purpose of forming such a government would not be fulfilled. This is because the person would be a political figure, which would further complicate matters.

According to him, an election-time non-party government is necessary. It must be formed on the basis of consensus. There is agreement on several issues in the proposal outlined in the July Charter. What is needed now is political goodwill. If this goodwill is not demonstrated, the country could face a grave crisis, he added.

item.title: 71 killed in Khulna in 10 months as nine criminal gangs remain active
item.description:
Sometimes people are shot dead in public, sometimes hacked or injured with sharp weapons, and at other times gunmen enter homes and open fire. Firearms are also being used in crimes such as mugging. From January to 23 October this year, 71 people were killed in Khulna city and district over a period of nearly 10 months. Of them, 23 were shot dead. The others were killed by hacking or beating.

A total of 69 murder cases were filed in Khulna city and district during the period in connection with the 71 deaths. The number of cases was lower than the death toll because three people were killed in a single incident. According to police, the killings were linked to drug trafficking, control over extortion, mugging, past enmities and rivalries between criminal gangs.

Most recently, two murders took place in Khulna city within 15 hours on 22 October. In the morning, a young man named Tawhidul Islam was shot dead in the Purba Baniakhamar area. In the evening, housewife Khushi Akter was shot dead by assailants near her home in the Jinnahpara area.

Police initially suspect that drug-related disputes were behind both killings. Investigators are also examining whether the two incidents were connected.

In recent months, Khulna city and district have witnessed a series of shootings, gun attacks causing injuries and other armed assaults. Ordinary citizens, political party leaders and activists, teachers, schoolgirls, women and pedestrians have also been targeted. Although law enforcement agencies say they are recovering illegal firearms and arresting criminals, the killings continue unabated.

SM Shafiqul Alam Mona, president of the Khulna city BNP, said they had urged the inspector general of police and other relevant authorities to improve the law and order situation.

If teen gangs, drugs and terrorism could not be eliminated, Khulna would face a dangerous situation, he said. He added that strict action would also be taken against anyone from his party involved in drug trafficking or other criminal activities.

Nine criminal gangs in focus

The names of nine criminal gangs have repeatedly surfaced in connection with many of the recent crimes in Khulna. They have become so brazen that they do not hesitate to open fire in public, even in crowded areas.

Several police sources said the active criminal groups in Khulna include B Company, led by Rony Chowdhury, also known as Grenade Babu; the Palash Group, led by Sheikh Palash; the Nur Azim Group; the Ashik Bahini; the Huma Bahini, led by Humayun Kabir; the Tengki Shawon Group, led by Sheikh Saidur Rahman, also known as Shawon; the Arman Group, led by Arman Sheikh; the Shakil Group, led by Shakil Sheikh; and the Nasim Group.

According to law enforcement sources, the Babu group holds sway across Khulna city. The Nur Azim and Ashik groups dominate the Khulna Sadar and Labanchara police station areas. The Shawon group is active in Sonadanga and Khalishpur, while the Arman Group and Huma Bahini have influence in the Daulatpur and Khan Jahan Ali police station areas.

Nasimul Gani, head of the Nasim Group, was shot dead in Dighalia upazila on 4 October.

Khulna Sadar, Labanchara and Harintana have witnessed a higher number of shootings and killings in recent months.

Mohammad Ahaduzzaman Mia, deputy commissioner of the Khulna Metropolitan Police's Detective Branch, told Prothom Alo that drug-related disputes were behind most of the killings. Police arrest listed criminals, but some of them become reckless again after securing bail. Ordinary people are also reluctant to speak out against criminals, which is another major problem, he said.

Meanwhile, several senior sources in the Khulna District Police said small armed groups were active in Dighalia, Aranghata, Koyra, Paikgachha and Dumuria. Some of these groups are accused of involvement in drug and arms trafficking. They frequently clash over local dominance, land, fish enclosures, sand businesses, transport and control over contract work.

Two murders in one day

Two murders took place in Khulna city on the morning and evening of 22 October. Tawhidul Islam was killed in the morning, while Khushi Akter was murdered later that evening.

Sources involved in the police investigations said Tawhidul was a member of the Palash Group, which has a rivalry with Rony Chowdhury Babu's group, known as Grenade Babu's group or B Company. Police also have information that Khushi Akter sold drugs on behalf of the Grenade Babu group.

Police filed a case over Tawhidul's murder. The first information report (FIR) mentions that B Company members Shahidul Islam, also known as Sejan; Sakibur Rahman, also known as Jitu; and Rabbi Chowdhury may have been involved.

In Khushi's murder case, her sister, Hashi Akter, filed a complaint naming four people, including top criminal Ashik.

Sheikh Palash, head of the Palash Group, was once involved in Chhatra League politics. The student organisation is now banned. His rise began after the 5 January 2014 general election.

According to local sources, Palash became influential through his close ties with Mohammad Mizanur Rahman, who was then the member of parliament for the Khulna-2 constituency. He subsequently built his own gang.

Palash was arrested in April 2015 and spent some time in prison.

Sources familiar with the matter said that after 5 August 2024, Palash's gang became involved in extortion in several areas of Khulna, including Mistripara, Banargati, Arambagh, Nirala, Paschim Baniakhamar, Rupsha Bagmara and Sonadanga. This led to a conflict with Grenade Babu. The two sides were involved in several killings in their struggle for control of the criminal underworld.

On 30 March 2025, a joint forces operation in Sonadanga, Khulna, resulted in the arrest of Sheikh Palash and 10 of his associates, along with weapons. He has remained in prison since then. Some of his followers have been killed, while others have joined the Nur Azim and Ashik groups in his absence.

Grenade Babu, meanwhile, faces at least 17 cases in different police stations, including murder, attempted murder and assault.

Nur Azim, the head of another group, had been in prison since January 2025. After securing bail in the final week of August this year, his group's activities increased in several areas of Khulna.

Police said members of the Nur Azim and Grenade Babu groups were collecting extortion money from various establishments. There have also been reports of one group extorting money while using the name of another.

69 murder cases

A total of 69 murder cases were filed in Khulna between January and 23 October this year, a period of nearly 10 months. This amounts to an average of one murder case every four days.

An analysis of Khulna Metropolitan Police (KMP) statistics shows that 34 murder cases were filed in the city between 1 January and 23 October, with 36 people killed in these incidents.

The number of murder cases in the city was 15 in 2021, 19 in 2022, 17 in 2023, 29 in 2024 and 34 in 2025.

The number of killings in areas under the District Police has also been alarming. According to district police figures, 30 murder cases were filed in 2021, 22 in 2022, 21 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 49 in 2025. By 23 October this year, the number had reached 35.

Discussions with relevant police officials revealed that at least 30 attempted murder incidents had also taken place in the district, apart from the killings. Firearms and sharp weapons were allegedly used in these incidents as well.

Use of illegal firearms on the rise

The use of illegal firearms has increased in Khulna. Law enforcement officials suspect that the weapons are entering the country through border routes.

According to KMP data, of the 34 murder cases filed in the city up to 23 October this year, 14 involved shootings. Drug trafficking and disputes over territorial dominance featured in these cases.

In areas under the District Police, firearms were reportedly used in nine of the 35 murder cases. Outside the city, police found direct links between criminal groups and six killings. District Police data also indicate that five killings were linked to drug trafficking and struggles for dominance.

Three senior KMP officers told Prothom Alo that some groups involved in drug trafficking provide their dealers and associates with motorcycles, monthly salaries, commissions and firearms.

Disputes over control of the drug trade can quickly escalate into armed clashes. The easy availability of weapons is also making criminals more reckless, they said.

According to police data, 24 firearms were recovered in KMP areas in 2024 and 47 in 2025. From January to September this year, police recovered 50 firearms and 233 bullets. The recovered weapons included 30 foreign-made pistols and seven foreign-made revolvers.

Forty-three cases were filed under the Arms Act in connection with these recoveries, and 75 people were arrested.

Detective Branch officers said many of the recovered weapons looked similar and most appeared to have been manufactured in India. The firearms were found to be operational. The city detective police estimate that at least 300 illegal firearms remain in circulation in Khulna city.

The district police also recovered 26 firearms and 53 bullets between January and September this year. Eighteen cases were filed in connection with these recoveries, naming 38 people as accused.

Ordinary people fall victim to gun violence

From the beginning of this year to 24 October, political party leaders and activists, businesspeople, women, teachers, schoolgirls and pedestrians were among those affected by shootings in different parts of Khulna city and district.

Dhananjay Kundu, also known as Akash Kundu, a college teacher from South Tutpara in Khulna city, runs a business alongside his teaching job. He was shot at his own shop in the Gachhtala area on 24 October. Police said the incident was linked to an extortion demand.

At midnight on 18 October, a young man named Sheikh Zumman Rahman was shot at the Tutpara Amtala intersection. Assailants arrived on a motorcycle, shot him and snatched his mobile phone.

Earlier, on the evening of 3 July, a 15-year-old Class X student was shot in the Rupsha Notun Bazar embankment road area of Khulna city. On 2 July, a young man named Ratul Sheikh was injured in a shooting by assailants at Ashibigha Balu Math in the Labanchara police station area.

Sources involved in the police investigations said the shootings had different causes. Some stemmed from personal disputes, others from extortion, mugging or conflicts over drug trafficking.

Kudrat-e-Khuda, general secretary of the Khulna district unit of Shushashoner Jonno Nagorik (SHUJAN), told Prothom Alo that shortcomings in police performance had contributed to the deterioration of the law and order situation.

Khulna was once known as a peaceful city, he said. The series of killings taking place now was beyond what people could have imagined.

item.title: Death penalty in Saudi Arabia: What does the law say, and what happens in court?
item.description:
The number of executions in Saudi Arabia is rising at an alarming rate. Recently, two Bangladeshis were executed. In the first six months of this year, Saudi Arabia executed 59 foreign nationals. Questions have repeatedly been raised about the death penalty for drug-related offences, the impact of capital punishment on foreign nationals, and the transparency of judicial proceedings.

Amid concerns over allegations of torture, restrictions on access to lawyers, and defendants’ opportunities to defend themselves, the country’s judicial system and its use of the death penalty have once again come under scrutiny. This is the first instalment of a report examining what the country’s laws say and what happens in its courts.

September 2025. Four Egyptian prisoners in a Saudi Arabian jail were told that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had reportedly ordered their executions to be suspended and that their cases would be reviewed. Prison authorities had given them this assurance. But shortly afterwards, without any prior notice, all four were executed.

This instance has now become all too familiar to readers in Bangladesh. Recently, two Bangladeshis convicted of committing an “immoral act” at a mosque in the holy city of Makkah were executed. According to the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR), an international human rights organisation, at least 108 people were executed in Saudi Arabia in the first six months of this year. The two Bangladeshis are not included in that figure. It is not known how many Bangladeshis were executed during those six months.

For many years, Saudi Arabia has been one of the countries carrying out the highest number of executions in the world. As in recent years, it is again near the top of the global rankings.

This raises several questions: Under which laws, at whose discretion, and in what kind of courts is a person sentenced to death? And what has become of the repeated promises of reform made by the crown prince? Let us examine the answers.

Nearly fourfold Increase in a decade

A record 356 executions were carried out in Saudi Arabia in 2025. A year earlier, in 2024, the number was 345, then the highest in a decade. In 2018, the year after Mohammed bin Salman became crown prince, 149 people were executed. The 2024 figure was more than double that number. Compared with the 90 executions recorded in 2014, the figure had risen nearly fourfold.

In the first six months of 2025 alone, 180 people were executed in Saudi Arabia. Amnesty International warned at the time that, if the trend continued, the annual total could approach the record set in 2024.

By the end of the year, however, the figure of 356 had surpassed even that record. From January 2014 to June 2025, a total of 1,816 people were executed in Saudi Arabia. Nearly one in every three was sentenced to death solely for a drug-related offence. Human rights organisations say the actual number is higher.

In the first six months of the current year, 2026, ESOHR recorded at least 108 executions. According to the organisation, the total number of executions carried out under King Salman bin Abdulaziz and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has reached 2,000. This is a record compared with any previous reign.

A record 356 executions were carried out in Saudi Arabia in 2025. A year earlier, in 2024, the number was 345, then the highest in a decade. In 2018, the year after Mohammed bin Salman became crown prince, 149 people were executed. The 2024 figure was more than double that number. Compared with the 90 executions recorded in 2014, the figure had risen nearly fourfold.

The final word rests with the judge

Saudi Arabia does not have a comprehensive penal code that defines all crimes and their corresponding punishments. Judges have broad discretion to determine what constitutes a crime and what punishment it warrants.

They do so based on their own interpretations of Islamic law, or Sharia, and fiqh—the understanding developed by Islamic jurists concerning the interpretation and application of Sharia provisions. Under the country’s system of governance, the Holy Quran and the Sunnah are the ultimate sources of all law.

Under Islamic law, crimes are divided into three categories: hudud, qisas and ta’zir. Punishments for the first two categories are prescribed, and they include the death penalty. Hudud refers to prescribed punishments for certain offences, including, in some circumstances, theft, adultery and drinking alcohol. Qisas applies mainly to murder or physical injury and involves retributive punishment. Under specific conditions, victims or the relatives of a deceased victim may grant forgiveness or accept compensation.

The third category, ta’zir, covers offences for which punishments are not prescribed under hudud or qisas. It includes acts that undermine public order or the interests of society. In these cases, the judge determines the punishment.

Bangladesh asks Saudi Arabia 6 questions over execution of 2 citizens

Death sentences in Saudi Arabia reflect a combination of punishments prescribed under Sharia and discretionary decisions under ta’zir. Despite being the harshest and most irreversible form of punishment, the death penalty is left to judicial discretion.

Saudi authorities say that capital punishment under ta’zir is “rarely applied”. However, statistics from human rights organisations paint a different picture.

Written laws also prescribe the death penalty for certain offences. The principal examples are the 2017 counterterrorism law and the 2005 anti-narcotics law. Under the anti-narcotics law, the death penalty is retained as the primary punishment for several offences.

Vague provisions of the counterterrorism law have also been used to sentence people to death on charges such as “endangering national unity”. For offences whose punishments are not specified in any law, judges turn to their interpretations of Sharia.

The list of offences punishable by death is also extensive. According to Amnesty International, the death penalty applies not only to murder but also to murder committed in connection with armed robbery, kidnapping or rape.

In addition, offences such as treason, rape, kidnapping, witchcraft and sorcery, robbery, torture and attempted murder may carry the death penalty. In drug-related cases, the penalty may apply to trafficking, possession, distribution and even consumption.

Under international law, however, the death penalty is permissible only for the “most serious crimes”, such as intentional murder. The Saudi government has told the relevant United Nations body that it imposes the death penalty only for the “most serious crimes”.

In February 2021, Saudi authorities announced a draft of a new law titled the Penal Code for Discretionary Sanctions, which was intended to codify ta’zir offences. After analysing a leaked draft, Amnesty International said that, rather than restricting the death penalty, the proposed law would further entrench it. Under the draft, judges would be able to impose death sentences for murder, rape and charges of “blasphemy” and “apostasy”. The draft has not yet been formally passed or brought into force.

Saudi researcher Abdullah AlaoudhThe crown prince has turned the judicial system into an instrument of his own control. To this end, he transferred prosecutorial powers—the administrative and legal authority to investigate cases on behalf of the state and bring defendants to trial—from the Interior Ministry to the royal court.

Who appoints the judges?

The country’s highest judicial body is the Supreme Judicial Council. It has 11 members and is headed by the justice minister. The king appoints its members for renewable four-year terms. Under the 2007 Law of the Judiciary, the council oversees the work of courts and judges. The Supreme Court is responsible for reviewing verdicts involving the death penalty, amputation, stoning to death and qisas.

The law provides for judicial independence, but according to Amnesty International, judges effectively remain under the control of the executive branch. Judges are appointed by royal decree. Although the law does not explicitly state that judges must be men, all judges in the country are male.

Both the Public Prosecution and the state security forces are directly accountable to the king and the crown prince. Saudi researcher Abdullah Alaoudh says the crown prince has turned the judicial system into an instrument of his own control. To this end, he transferred prosecutorial powers—the administrative and legal authority to investigate cases on behalf of the state and bring defendants to trial—from the Interior Ministry to the royal court. He has also removed potential rivals who could exert influence over the judiciary and filled courts with loyalists.

According to Amnesty International, the authorities have been able to use the courts to punish critics of the government’s political and economic policies by exploiting judges’ broad discretionary powers and the lack of judicial independence.

Execution of 2 Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia: What does the consulate’s letter say?

Defendants’ rights do exist on paper. Under the Law of Criminal Procedure, issued by royal decree in November 2013, defendants have the right to legal assistance during both the investigation and trial stages.

Torture and other forms of ill-treatment of defendants are prohibited; limits are placed on the duration of pretrial detention; judicial review is mandatory in cases of prolonged detention; and appeals are permitted against all verdicts, including death sentences.

In practice, Amnesty International says, safeguards meeting international standards have not been consistently upheld, even in death penalty cases.

Cases involving allegations of terrorist activities and political offences are heard by the Specialised Criminal Court. The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has said that this court cannot be considered an independent and impartial tribunal.

Promises on paper, a different reality

Since 2018, Saudi authorities have repeatedly pledged to reform the use of the death penalty. According to Amnesty International, each time they have either backtracked or failed to implement reforms consistent with international standards.

In an interview with The Atlantic on 3 March 2022, the crown prince said that they had abolished everything related to the death penalty except for one category. That category, he said, was set out in the Holy Quran, and there was nothing they could do about it.

The crown prince has also repeatedly given public assurances that the death penalty would be retained only for murder and abolished for offences for which Sharia does not mandate capital punishment, such as drug-related crimes. In other words, death sentences would no longer be imposed on the basis of ta’zir. Yet announcements by the Saudi Press Agency itself indicate that executions for ta’zir offences continue.

In January 2021, Saudi Arabia’s Human Rights Commission announced on social media that executions for drug-related offences had been suspended. This unofficial moratorium was lifted in 2023, after which executions resumed in cases that had previously been put on hold.

Nearly half of all death sentences based on judicial discretion

Amnesty International analysed the legal basis for death sentences announced between January 2014 and June 2025. It found that 862 executions, or 47.5 per cent, were based on ta’zir. Of these, 597 (69.3 per cent) were solely for drug-related offences, while 135 (15.7 per cent) were solely for offences related to “terrorism”.

The figures over time reveal the following pattern: from 2014 to 2018, roughly half of all death sentences were based on hudud or qisas, with the other half based on ta’zir. In 2019, the share of ta’zir cases jumped to around 71 per cent. That year, the Saudi Press Agency reported 130 executions based on ta’zir, including 84 people executed solely for drug-related offences.

ESOHR has reported that another 49 people convicted over alleged peaceful expressions of dissent are now at risk of execution. They include Sheikh Salman al-Awda and Sheikh Hassan al-Maliki. Public prosecutors have been seeking the death penalty for them since 2018, but their trials remain unresolved to this day.

The proportion of ta’zir-based executions fell between 2020 and 2023, which Amnesty International believes may partly be attributable to the moratorium on executions for drug-related offences.

In 2024, however, 40.9 per cent of executions were again carried out on the basis of ta’zir, while the legal basis for another 11.3 per cent remained unknown. That year, 122 people were executed under ta’zir solely for drug-related offences, nearly twice the figure for 2015. From January to June 2025 alone, the number stood at 118.

An expansive definition of ‘terrorism’ and the punishment of dissent

Alongside drug-related offences, “terrorism” is the second major category. According to Amnesty International, Saudi Arabia uses extremely vague definitions of “terrorism”, “terrorist offences” and “terrorist organisations” to impose death sentences even in cases that do not involve intentional killing. The aim, the organisation says, is to suppress dissent.

Using vague provisions of the 2017 counterterrorism law, judges have imposed death sentences for charges such as “endangering national unity” and “undermining public order and the security of society”. Amnesty International says that peaceful expressions of dissent, human rights advocacy and campaigning for political reform have also been treated as crimes against the state or as “terrorism”.

When anti-discrimination protests intensified in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province in 2011–2012, the authorities cracked down on people suspected of participating in or supporting the demonstrations. Many protesters were arrested, including minors. The death penalty was used as a punishment.

One of the most prominent cases in this category is that of Saud al-Faraj. The businessman was arrested in December 2019 on allegations of involvement in protests in Al-Qatif. He was sentenced to death in 2022 for participating in the 2011–2012 protests. His execution was carried out in June this year. The United Nations Working Group had previously deemed his detention unlawful and arbitrary.

ESOHR has reported that another 49 people convicted over alleged peaceful expressions of dissent are now at risk of execution. They include Sheikh Salman al-Awda and Sheikh Hassan al-Maliki. Public prosecutors have been seeking the death penalty for them since 2018, but their trials remain unresolved to this day.

This year’s figures: 83 of 108 executions not linked to murder

In 2026, of the 108 executions documented by ESOHR, 84, or 77.7 per cent, were carried out on the basis of ta’zir. By category of offence, 71 executions (65.7 per cent) were for drug-related crimes, 25 (23 per cent) for murder, nine (around 8 per cent) in political and security-related cases, and three in other cases.

In other words, 83 of the 108 executions were for offences unrelated to murder.

ESOHR also reported that, before the executions were carried out, neither the organisation nor any other organisation had been able to obtain or document information about 91 of the 108 cases (84.2 per cent).

What happens in court?

In every case documented by human rights organisations, defendants have alleged that they were subjected to torture or ill-treatment during interrogation to extract confessions, which were subsequently admitted in court as evidence against them.

According to these organisations, most death sentences and convictions in Saudi Arabia are based solely on coerced confessions. In the cases they examined or verified, allegations of torture were dismissed without any investigation.

The allegations made by Saud al-Faraj are even more disturbing. He was repeatedly tortured because he refused to sign a false confession. He was beaten so severely that he had to be hospitalised, subjected to sexual violence, and his wife was threatened with gang rape.

She was also forced to sign a statement against her husband under the threat of having their young child taken away. During his trial, he detailed the allegations of torture and submitted written complaints to the Specialised Criminal Court, the Public Prosecution, the Saudi Human Rights Commission and the crown prince himself. No investigation was initiated, and the court did not examine whether his confession was admissible.

Jalal al-Labbad was sentenced to death for participating in protests in Al-Qatif when he was a minor. He was allegedly tortured through electric shocks, suffocation and beatings, and held in prolonged solitary confinement to force him to sign false statements.

In several cases, including those of five young men sentenced to death for participating in protests during childhood, confessions extracted through torture were accepted as the sole evidence leading to conviction.

Detention in isolation, cut off from the outside world, makes it easier to extract such coerced confessions. After his arrest on 2 December 2019, Saud al-Faraj spent more than 20 months in solitary confinement, without any contact with anyone outside.

Jalal al-Labbad was held in solitary confinement for a total of nine months over two separate periods. Abdullah al-Derazi was cut off from the outside world for three months, and his family did not know where he was.

Yusuf al-Manasif’s family was unable to visit him for five months after his arrest. Jawad Qureiris had no access to either a lawyer or his family during the investigation. Hassan Zaki al-Faraj spent three months in solitary confinement, while Farhat Abu al-Saud was held in isolation for four months.

During his solitary confinement, Mohammed Labbad was beaten by several people at once with metal wires. He was kicked on various parts of his body, including his genitals, and suffocated by having a foot pressed against his throat. He was subjected to waterboarding and kept shackled at his hands and feet for prolonged periods.

The United Nations Special Rapporteur on torture has repeatedly stated that no one should be convicted solely on the basis of a confession. According to the Working Group, coerced confessions taint the entire judicial process and seriously undermine the fundamental principles of a fair trial.

Expatriates bear a disproportionate burden

The burden of this judicial system does not fall equally on everyone. Of Saudi Arabia’s population of approximately 35.3 million, around 15.7 million are expatriates or foreign nationals, accounting for 44.4 per cent. Yet of the 122 executions carried out solely for drug-related offences in 2024, 92—or 75.4 per cent—involved foreign nationals.

In 2025, at least 188 of the 240 executions for drug-related offences involved foreign nationals. In the first half of the current year, 59 of the 108 people executed—around 54 per cent—were foreign nationals. They included citizens of 17 countries, including Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia.

In 2023, the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination expressed particular concern over the “significant increase” in executions since 2023 and called for a moratorium on the death penalty. Two UN special rapporteurs also sent a joint letter to the Saudi government expressing concern over the potentially discriminatory application of the death penalty against foreign nationals convicted of drug-related offences.

Death row prisoners awaiting execution

Conditions in Saudi prisons, particularly for prisoners sentenced to death, are especially poor. They include overcrowding, unhygienic conditions and administrative neglect, including inadequate medical care.

Before their executions, prisoners at Tabuk Prison were held in cramped, dirty cells with poor ventilation. On 18 February 2025, several prisoners began a hunger strike. They were protesting restrictions on contact with their families and degrading treatment, including being made to walk barefoot in handcuffs when being transferred for medical care.

Saudi law contains no explicit provision requiring prisoners or their families to be notified in advance of an execution, nor does it guarantee the return of the body. In practice, families may learn that a loved one is about to be executed only 24 hours beforehand. Prisoners have interpreted the transfer of foreign inmates convicted of similar offences to isolated wards as a sign that executions are imminent.

Amnesty International found that, in the cases of three people executed during the first half of 2025, their bodies were not returned to their families, and the locations of their graves were not disclosed.

Even prisoners who believe their cases are still under review have been executed. Jordanian national Hussein Abu al-Khair had been asked by Saudi prison authorities to appoint a lawyer in preparation for a retrial. Shortly afterwards, he was executed.

In June 2021, Abu al-Khair told his family that he had been informed that his “sentence had been suspended and was being reviewed by the Ministry of Interior under a royal directive, in connection with the pardon of some prisoners convicted of drug offences”. Although the sentences of several people around him were commuted, he remained in detention. In March 2023, he was executed without prior notice.

The consequences of such assurances followed by sudden executions are not limited to the prisoners themselves. The same thing happened to the four Egyptian prisoners mentioned at the beginning of this report: after being assured that the crown prince had ordered their executions suspended, they were suddenly put to death. Such false assurances cause intense psychological anguish for prisoners and their families.

Prisoners interviewed by ESOHR said they live in constant fear of execution. In recent months, they have witnessed death-row inmates being completely separated from others for a period of time, cut off from the outside world and then suddenly taken away for execution.

UN recommendations and international obligations

During a United Nations Universal Periodic Review in 2024, at least 35 recommendations were made concerning the death penalty in Saudi Arabia. Several countries called on the kingdom to move towards abolishing capital punishment by introducing a formal moratorium. Argentina recommended explicitly prohibiting the death penalty for offences committed by people under the age of 18.

Amnesty International has called on Saudi Arabia to conduct an immediate, independent and transparent investigation into discrimination in the application of the death penalty. Under the Convention against Torture, Saudi Arabia is obliged to prevent torture and ensure that confessions obtained through torture are not admitted in legal proceedings.

Yet the picture in the first six months of 2026 once again makes clear that Saudi Arabia continues to carry out executions at a rapid pace, without regard for its international obligations or publicly declared legal commitments. These include its commitments under the Convention against Torture and the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Despite growing international criticism and serious concerns over unfair trials, torture, discrimination and a lack of transparency, the country appears determined to maintain its position among the world’s leading executioners.

Hussein Abu al-Khair’s sister told Amnesty International that her brother’s execution came after “nine years of torture”. He endured that suffering, as did his wife, children and the rest of his family. With his body never returned, the family had nothing with which to mourn him. After this long accounting of laws, courts and promised reforms, one question remains: in a country carrying out executions at record levels, does a person’s final news even reach their family in time?

Sources

1. World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), Law of Criminal Procedure (promulgated by Royal Decree No. M/39 of 28 Rajab 1422 [16 October 2001]), Saudi Arabia.

2. Joint report by three human rights organisations—the MENA Rights Group, ALQST for Human Rights and the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR)—Death Penalty in Saudi Arabia: Joint Submission to the Special Rapporteur on Extrajudicial, Summary or Arbitrary Executions, 10 March 2026.

3. Amnesty International, Saudi Arabia: “If We Had Money and a Lawyer, Maybe My Brother Would Be Alive”: Saudi Arabia’s Execution Crisis, 7 July 2025.

4. European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR), 108 Saudi Arabia: Executions in the First Half of 2026.
